title: Ranked from Within: Ranking Large Multimodal Models Without Labels
authors: Weijie Tu; Weijian Deng; Dylan Campbell; Yu Yao; Jiyang Zheng; Tom Gedeon; Tongliang Liu
venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning
subtopics: unsupervised model ranking; uncertainty; LMM
summary: Studies whether large multimodal models can be ranked without labels, evaluating 47 models on 9 VQA benchmarks, and finds softmax-based uncertainty scores give robust unsupervised rankings.
relation_to_specdx: It is label-free model assessment, relevant to choosing SpecDx's 'best single interpreter' (B2) without gold.

title: Optimality of Belief Propagation for Crowdsourced Classification
authors: Jungseul Ok; Sewoong Oh; Jinwoo Shin; Yung Yi
venue: Proceedings of The 33rd International Conference on Machine Learning
subtopics: belief propagation optimality; Dawid-Skene
summary: Proves that belief propagation exactly matches a tightened fundamental limit for Dawid-Skene label recovery when each worker gets at most two tasks, and dominates other provable algorithms in general.
relation_to_specdx: It is theory context for optimal inference under the DS model.

title: Variational Inference for Crowdsourcing
authors: Qiang Liu; Jian Peng; Alex Ihler
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems
subtopics: belief propagation; mean field; priors on reliability
summary: Casts crowd label aggregation as graphical-model inference and applies BP and mean field. BP generalises majority vote and KOS, and MF relates to EM. Performance hinges on the prior over worker reliability.
relation_to_specdx: It shows the prior matters, as do SpecDx's Dirichlet error-pool prior and MAP fitting. It is a possible alternative inference engine.

title: Learning from Partial Labels
authors: Timothee Cour; Ben Sapp; Ben Taskar
venue: Journal of Machine Learning Research
subtopics: partial labels; candidate label sets; disambiguation
summary: Studies multiclass learning when each instance has a candidate set of labels of which only one is correct, characterises when learning is possible via a data-distribution property, and gives a convex learning formulation.
relation_to_specdx: Set-valued supervision with one hidden true label is related to, but opposite from, SpecDx's set-valued truth, where every element of A_c is genuinely entailed.

title: Cheap and fast---but is it good?: evaluating non-expert annotations for natural language tasks
authors: Rion Snow; Brendan O'Connor; Daniel Jurafsky; Andrew Y. Ng
venue: Proceedings of the 2008 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP '08)
subtopics: crowdsourcing; non-expert annotation; bias correction
summary: Shows on five NLP tasks that Mechanical Turk non-expert annotations agree well with expert gold labels, and proposes a bias-correction technique that improves aggregate annotation quality.
relation_to_specdx: It is the historical precedent for replacing an expert with a crowd of cheap fallible annotators. SpecDx makes the same move with local LLMs and uses the crowd to audit the 'gold' itself.

title: Are “Solved Issues” in SWE-bench Really Solved Correctly? An Empirical Study
authors: You Wang; Michael Pradel; Zhongxin Liu
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering
subtopics: weak tests; SWE-bench Verified; differential patch testing; plausible but incorrect patches; weak test oracles; plausible patches; differential testing; SWE-bench; weak checks
summary: Introduces PatchDiff, differential patch testing that exposes behavioural differences between a generated patch and the ground-truth patch, and finds on SWE-bench Verified that 7.8% of 'correct' patches fail the developer test suite and 29.6% of plausible patches behave differently from the ground truth.
relation_to_specdx: Evidence and a technique for the weak-check class in a top SE venue: differential testing produces a witness input where a passing behaviour diverges from the intended one, similar in spirit to SpecDx's witness-based refutation; it requires a reference patch, whereas SpecDx works from the NL specification and an executor population. | Quantifies weak checks in an agent benchmark and uses behavioural witnesses (differentiating inputs), similar in spirit to SpecDx's witness-backed refutation. | Differential testing produces witnesses that a check is too weak (a passing behaviour that differs from intended), the analogue of SpecDx's weak-check refutation; it compares to a single reference patch rather than to the consensus of an interpreter population.

title: Auditing LLM Benchmarks with Item Response Theory
authors: Sander Land; Daniel M. Bikel
venue: arXiv
subtopics: IRT benchmark auditing; mislabel detection; negative discrimination; reward-model benchmarks; ambiguous items; model x item matrix
specdx_components: item difficulty/IRT; identifiability; baseline B3; real-defect benchmark; defect taxonomy; anchored cell model
summary: Introduces an IRT mislabel indicator, fitted on responses of 114 models, that surfaces likely mislabels at 95% precision in the top 200 items across seven preference and multiple-choice benchmarks (beating a supervised classifier); the indicator is a forced-ceiling likelihood ratio from a constrained 4PL fit that asks whether stronger models become increasingly correct or increasingly incorrect on an item. Errors are traced to mechanical labelling heuristics, inherited upstream annotation mistakes and inherently ambiguous items. Accepted at EMNLP 2026 (arXiv comment); flagged items released on Hugging Face (Writer/IRT-mislabeled-items).
relation_to_specdx: The closest 'statistics-only' competitor and the published counterpart of B3: a population of models plus IRT flags items whose key is wrong, using the same 'accuracy gradient' intuition as SpecDx (does correctness rise or fall with model ability?), and it notes that the indicator needs enough ability spread for θ to be identifiable. It treats each item as single-label with a fixed key, gives a ranked untyped flag without localisation or witnesses, and has no logic layer (no MUS/MCS, contradiction, weak-check detection or refutation). | It is the closest competitor for the statistical half of SpecDx: a population of models audits a fallible answer key and finds both mis-keys and ambiguous items. It differs in four ways: it works on static QA labels rather than executable specifications, has no set-valued truth or anchor-as-rater model, has no MUS/MCS contradiction analysis, and gives no refutation witnesses or localisation in T. It is the published counterpart of baseline B3.
baseline_notes: Same input shape as SpecDx's interpreter × clause (or × cell) 0/1 matrix scored against the declared value d_c. Implement B3 in two variants with py-irt or a small PyTorch fit: (a) plain 2PL, rank items by negative/low discrimination a_i (the paper reports this variant trails); (b) the paper's forced-ceiling indicator: fit the constrained 3PL-style model (c_i = chance floor, e.g. 1/|candidate values| for cells or 0 for clauses; d_i = 1; per-subset discrimination; b_i bounded) and compute the likelihood-ratio Δℓ_i against a free ceiling d_i, ranking items whose strong interpreters systematically miss d_c. Expect it to catch hidden-requirement/mis-key cells, but not weak checks (everyone passes) or contradictions (everyone fails, so no ability gradient); with only a handful of local model families the θ spread may be too small, which is exactly the identifiability regime SpecDx's theory addresses. No code repository found (only the dataset), so B3 must be re-implemented from the paper's equations. | This is B3 itself: fit a 2PL IRT on the interpreter x clause (or cell) correctness matrix, scoring correctness against d_c, and flag items with negative discrimination or the paper's mislabel indicator. Data is released on Hugging Face (per the arXiv comment); no code repository was verified. It can be re-implemented with py-irt or a few lines of PyTorch, offline.

title: Automated Benchmark Auditing for AI Agents and Large Language Models
authors: Junlin Wang; Federico Bianchi; Shang Zhu; Fan Nie; Yongchan Kwon; Bhuwan Dhingra; James Zou
venue: arXiv
subtopics: automated benchmark auditing; agentic auditor; specification gaps; incorrect ground truth; ambiguous tasks
specdx_components: defect taxonomy; real-defect benchmark; baseline B1
summary: Auto Benchmark Audit (ABA) is an agentic LLM framework that audits individual benchmark tasks for hidden environment dependencies, specification gaps and limited grading logic; over 168 benchmarks in nine domains it flags critical issues (ambiguous design, environment conflicts, incorrect ground truth) in over 25.7% of tasks, validated by experts and upstream PRs, and filtering them shifts rankings and raises SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2 scores by about 10%.
relation_to_specdx: Fully automatic detection of specification gaps, ambiguity and wrong ground truth in benchmarks, so it threatens SpecDx's 'automatic' claim; but it is a single (frontier) LLM auditor reasoning over artefacts, i.e. a strong version of static review B1, with no executor-population statistics, no identifiability argument and no logical refutation or witnesses. | Directly targets specification and check defects in agent tasks, automatically, and validates against upstream fixes. ABA is a per-task LLM agent audit; SpecDx instead infers defects from the statistics of many fallible executors and confirms them with logical witnesses, and it types defects by satisfaction (contradiction, hidden requirement, ambiguity, weak check).
baseline_notes: Published counterpart of B1 (static LLM review). Code and annotations are said to be released (autobenchaudit.com; GitHub IsThatYou/auto-bench-audit per its release page); it would take T (policy, task text, tool descriptions) plus C (evaluation script / golden state) per task and output issue reports, which can be mapped to SpecDx's four defect types. It calls frontier API models by default, so an offline run requires swapping in local models. Repository confirmed with lit.py github (no licence declared). | Released agentic auditor and task annotations. Adapt by packaging each SpecDx scenario as a task directory (instructions = T, environment = DB + tools, grader = C) and running ABA; map its issue labels onto SpecDx's four defect types and compare precision/recall per cell. Needs an LLM agent backend; check whether it supports local models.

title: Policy Loopholes in Agent Evaluation: When Policy Ambiguity Masquerades as Agent Error
authors: Hongliu Cao
venue: arXiv
subtopics: policy ambiguity; τ²-bench audit; agent evaluation validity; contradiction; multiple defensible readings
specdx_components: defect taxonomy; real-defect benchmark; family effects/correlated errors
summary: Argues that agent benchmarks wrongly assume each natural-language policy determines a unique correct action; audits two τ²-bench domains, builds a taxonomy of policy loopholes (silence, ambiguity, contradiction), and shows that affected tasks lower scores in model-specific ways and reduce every model's consistency across trials, with exploitability requiring both policy ambiguity and tool permissiveness. Accepted at the REALM workshop at EMNLP 2026 (arXiv comment).
relation_to_specdx: Directly threatens the 'ambiguity/contradiction in T' part of SpecDx's taxonomy on the same τ²-bench source, and uses cross-model inconsistency as its symptom. It is a manual audit with a qualitative taxonomy; SpecDx detects and types such defects automatically, localises the ambiguous sentences by ddmin, and certifies contradictions with MUS/MCS and witness states.
baseline_notes: No released code found; the method is a manual audit, so it can serve as a source of labelled real defects (τ²-bench airline/retail loopholes) rather than a runnable baseline.

title: SWE-ABS: Adversarial Benchmark Strengthening Exposes Inflated Success Rates on Test-based Benchmark
authors: Boxi Yu; Yang Cao; Yuzhong Zhang; Liting Lin; Junjielong Xu; Zhiqing Zhong; Qinghua Xu; Guancheng Wang; Jialun Cao; Shing-Chi Cheung; Pinjia He; Lionel Briand
venue: arXiv
subtopics: weak tests; SWE-bench Verified; adversarial test augmentation; mutation testing
specdx_components: defect taxonomy; mutation evaluation; real-defect benchmark; refutation
summary: SWE-ABS strengthens SWE-bench test suites by coverage-driven augmentation with program slicing and by mutation-driven adversarial testing that synthesises plausible but wrong patches; on SWE-bench Verified it strengthens 50.2% of instances, rejects 19.71% of previously passing patches, and drops the top agent from 78.80% to 62.20%.
relation_to_specdx: Shows at scale that one in five 'solved' patches pass only because the checks are weak, i.e. SpecDx's weak-check class, and uses synthesised wrong behaviours as kill witnesses much like SpecDx's mutation/refutation step; it repairs code-benchmark tests given a reference patch, while SpecDx diagnoses weak clauses in business specifications without a reference implementation.

title: Are LLMs Better than Reported? Detecting Label Errors and Mitigating Their Effect on Model Performance
authors: Omer Nahum; Nitay Calderon; Orgad Keller; Idan Szpektor; Roi Reichart
venue: Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
subtopics: LLM ensemble label error detection; LLM-as-a-judge; benchmark relabelling; LLM ensemble label-error detection; benchmark label quality
specdx_components: anchored cell model; family effects/correlated errors; baseline B4; baseline B2; real-defect benchmark
summary: Uses an ensemble of LLMs (LLM-as-a-judge with diverse prompts and confidence scores) to flag likely mislabeled examples in four TRUE factual-consistency datasets and SummEval, compares expert, crowd and LLM annotation, and finds substantial label errors whose correction raises reported model performance; larger ensembles and high-confidence disagreement with the gold label are stronger error signals.
relation_to_specdx: The nearest label-level analogue of SpecDx's core idea: a population of LLMs disagreeing confidently with the given label flags the label, not the models. It assumes one correct label per item, uses LLMs as judges rather than as executors of a specification, and has no model of interpreter accuracy, item difficulty, set-valued truth or logical refutation. | An LLM committee auditing a dataset's given labels (a fallible anchor) is SpecDx's setting restricted to static labels. Its confidence-thresholded ensemble vote is a simple baseline for SpecDx's mis-key detection.
baseline_notes: Simple to reproduce offline on SpecDx data: for each cell, compare the declared value d_c with the population's majority (or confidence-weighted) reading and flag when the ensemble's agreement against d_c exceeds a threshold; ensemble size and family composition are the knobs. This is essentially the 'anchor vs. majority' simulation baseline with confidence weighting. No repository verified.

title: Are We Done with MMLU?
authors: Aryo Pradipta Gema; Joshua Ong Jun Leang; Giwon Hong; Alessio Devoto; Alberto Carlo Maria Mancino; Rohit Saxena; Xuanli He; Yu Zhao; Xiaotang Du; Mohammad Reza Ghasemi Madani; Claire Barale; Robert McHardy; Joshua Harris; Jean Kaddour; Emile Van Krieken; Pasquale Minervini
venue: Proceedings of the 2025 Conference of the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Volume 1: Long Papers)
subtopics: MMLU errors; MMLU-Redux; error annotation protocol; benchmark repair
specdx_components: defect taxonomy; set-valued truth; real-defect benchmark
summary: Analyses ground-truth errors in MMLU with a hierarchical error-annotation protocol (bad question clarity, bad options clarity, no correct answer, multiple correct answers, wrong ground truth), finds e.g. 57% of analysed Virology questions erroneous, builds MMLU-Redux (5,700 manually re-annotated questions across 57 subjects), estimates 6.49% of MMLU questions contain errors, and shows that model metrics shift on the corrected set.
relation_to_specdx: Its error taxonomy maps onto SpecDx's classes for a single-answer benchmark: wrong ground truth ≈ mis-key, multiple correct answers ≈ ambiguity (set-valued truth), no correct answer ≈ contradiction/empty entailment set. Detection is manual re-annotation, which SpecDx replaces with an executor population and logic.

title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
authors: Shunyu Yao; Noah Shinn; Pedram Razavi; Karthik Narasimhan
venue: The Thirteenth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2025)
subtopics: agent benchmark; policy following; golden end state; pass^k; policy adherence; tool-agent-user benchmark; pass^k consistency
summary: τ-bench emulates conversations between an LLM-simulated user and a tool-using agent bound by domain policies (retail, airline), scores by comparing the final database state with an annotated goal state, and introduces pass^k for reliability; gpt-4o-class agents solve under 50% of tasks with pass^8 under 25% in retail.
relation_to_specdx: A prototypical executable business specification S = ⟨T, C, Π⟩: policies and tool descriptions are T, the golden end state is C, the tasks are Π. SpecDx treats this S as fallible, which later repairs (τ-Bench Verified, τ²-Bench-Verified, ABC's findings) confirm. | τ-bench is one of SpecDx's subjects: its policy text is T and its goal-state/expected-action checks are C. τ-bench treats S as ground truth; SpecDx asks when the goal state itself is defective, and its repeated-trial (pass^k) runs are exactly the population of executions SpecDx mines. | tau-bench is a direct instance of S = <T, C, Pi> (policy text, golden end state, scenarios) whose defects SpecDx targets; pass^k measures agent consistency but treats every repeated failure as the agent's, which is exactly the confound SpecDx separates.

title: Do Large Language Model Benchmarks Test Reliability?
authors: Joshua Vendrow; Edward Vendrow; Sara Beery; Aleksander Madry
venue: arXiv
subtopics: platinum benchmarks; label errors; ambiguity; reliability evaluation; benchmark repair
specdx_components: defect taxonomy; real-defect benchmark; set-valued truth
summary: Argues that LLM benchmarks do not measure reliability because pervasive label errors and ambiguity hide genuine model failures; proposes 'platinum' benchmarks curated to minimise label errors and ambiguity, revises examples from fifteen popular benchmarks, and finds that frontier LLMs still fail simple tasks such as elementary math word problems.
relation_to_specdx: Repairs benchmark items by flagging those where models disagree with the label and then manually removing mislabeled or ambiguous ones, i.e. a model-population-assisted manual audit; SpecDx automates the diagnosis, types the defect and keeps ambiguous items as set-valued truth instead of deleting them.

title: SABER: Small Actions, Big Errors -- Safeguarding Mutating Steps in LLM Agents
authors: Alejandro Cuadron; Pengfei Yu; Yang Liu; Arpit Gupta
venue: arXiv
subtopics: τ-bench Verified; τ²-Bench-Verified; annotation errors; underspecified tasks; agent safeguards
summary: Analyses τ-Bench (airline/retail) and SWE-bench Verified traces, finds that deviations in mutating (state-changing) actions drive failure, and proposes a test-time safeguard (SABER); it also identifies ceiling effects in τ-Bench caused by annotation errors and underspecified tasks and releases τ-Bench Verified with targeted revisions. This is the paper cited by the amazon-agi/tau2-bench-verified release, whose FIXES.md lists policy-compliance, database-accuracy, logical-consistency and evaluation-ambiguity fixes.
relation_to_specdx: The source of SpecDx's real-defect set (the τ²-Bench-Verified diff). The repairs were found manually from failure analysis; SpecDx aims to find the same contradictions, hidden requirements and ambiguities automatically.

title: Annotation Error Detection: Analyzing the Past and Present for a More Coherent Future
authors: Jan-Christoph Klie; Bonnie Webber; Iryna Gurevych
venue: Computational Linguistics
subtopics: annotation error detection; survey; benchmark of AED methods; benchmark of 18 methods
specdx_components: baseline B3; anchored cell model; real-defect benchmark; baseline B2
summary: Reimplements 18 annotation error detection methods and evaluates them on 9 English datasets for text classification and token/span labelling, defines a uniform formalisation, evaluation protocol and best practices for the task, and releases the datasets and implementations as an open-source package (nessie).
relation_to_specdx: The standard survey and toolkit for detecting wrong labels in a corpus; every method assumes one correct label per instance and needs a trained model or repeated annotations, whereas SpecDx diagnoses typed defects of an executable specification from interpreter behaviour. | Detecting errors in gold annotations is the dataset-level twin of detecting defects in a specification's checks. Its taxonomy (variation-based, model-based, training-dynamics) helps position SpecDx's population-of-interpreters approach.
baseline_notes: nessie (UKPLab/nessie, MIT, last push 2023) offers flaggers that take repeated annotations or model probabilities. On SpecDx data treat each interpreter reading of a cell as an annotation and d_c as the label under test; the 'variation' and 'ensemble/probability' flaggers (e.g. classification uncertainty, confident learning, KNN entropy, label aggregation) can then rank cells. Offline Python, but needs an adapter from the run log to its array format.

title: Is Your Code Generated by ChatGPT Really Correct? Rigorous Evaluation of Large Language Models for Code Generation
authors: Jiawei Liu; Chunqiu Steven Xia; Yuyao Wang; Lingming Zhang
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023)
subtopics: weak tests; code benchmarks; test augmentation; HumanEval+
specdx_components: defect taxonomy; mutation evaluation; real-defect benchmark
summary: EvalPlus augments code-generation benchmarks with large numbers of tests from LLM- and mutation-based input generation; extending HumanEval's tests 80× (HumanEval+) catches much previously undetected wrong code (pass@k drops by up to 19.3–28.9%) and reveals that test insufficiency mis-ranks models.
relation_to_specdx: Canonical evidence of the 'weak check' defect class: the benchmark's checks C are looser than its NL task T, so wrong programs pass. EvalPlus repairs C by test generation against a reference solution; SpecDx instead detects that C is weak by observing interpreter behaviours that pass every clause while diverging from T, without a reference implementation.

title: py-irt: A Scalable Item Response Theory Library for Python
authors: John Patrick Lalor; Pedro Rodriguez
venue: INFORMS Journal on Computing
subtopics: IRT software; Bayesian IRT; py-irt
summary: py-irt is a Python library, built on Pyro and PyTorch with GPU support, for fitting Bayesian IRT models (1PL, 2PL, 4PL and related) and ideal-point models to estimate latent subject and item traits at scale.
relation_to_specdx: The natural runnable implementation of baseline B3; it fits a single binary response matrix against a fixed key and has no notion of a fallible anchor, set-valued truth or defect type.
baseline_notes: Runs offline. Export the SpecDx run log as JSONL with one row per interpreter (subject_id = model×seed or model) and responses {cell_or_clause_id: 0/1}, where 1 = the reading equals the declared value d_c (cell data) or the behaviour satisfies the clause (clause data). Fit `py-irt train 2pl` (or 4pl), read item discrimination a_j and difficulty b_j, and rank cells/clauses by a_j < 0 (B3) or by low a_j with high b_j. Families can be added as covariates only by refitting per family. Code: nd-ball/py-irt, MIT, actively maintained.

title: Confident Learning: Estimating Uncertainty in Dataset Labels
authors: Curtis Northcutt; Lu Jiang; Isaac Chuang
venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research
subtopics: confident learning; label error detection; noisy labels; cleanlab; noisy given labels
specdx_components: anchored cell model; baseline B3; baseline B2
summary: Confident learning estimates the joint distribution between given (noisy) and latent true labels under a class-conditional noise assumption, using probabilistic thresholds, counting and ranking to find and prune label errors, with sufficient conditions for exact recovery.
relation_to_specdx: Formalises the 'given label is a noisy rater' view that SpecDx's anchor d_c also takes; CL needs out-of-sample predicted probabilities from a trained classifier and a single true class per example, while SpecDx uses an LLM population, a set-valued entailment set and a contradiction/empty-set case. | It is the closest ML analogue of treating the spec's declared value as a fallible anchor: CL flags given labels contradicted by model evidence. SpecDx uses a population of interpreters instead of one trained classifier and types the deviation (mis-key vs ambiguity vs contradiction).
baseline_notes: cleanlab.filter.find_label_issues(labels, pred_probs): per cell c, labels = index of the declared value d_c in the cell's candidate-value vocabulary; pred_probs = the empirical distribution of values read by the interpreter population (optionally family-weighted, with a smoothing pseudo-count). Flagged cells are those where the population confidently prefers another value: candidates for hidden requirement/mis-key. It cannot express ambiguity (two acceptable values) or weak checks without extra rules. Offline, pip-installable: cleanlab/cleanlab (Apache-2.0). | cleanlab.filter.find_label_issues with given_labels = d_c per cell and pred_probs = the empirical distribution of model readings per cell (or committee vote shares). It flags cells whose declared value is likely wrong, giving a mis-key/hidden-requirement detector. For the multi-annotator variant use cleanlab.multiannotator (CROWDLAB) with the spec as one annotator. Offline, pip install cleanlab.

title: Evaluation Examples are not Equally Informative: How should that change NLP Leaderboards?
authors: Pedro Rodriguez; Joe Barrow; Alexander Miserlis Hoyle; John P. Lalor; Robin Jia; Jordan Boyd-Graber
venue: Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers)
subtopics: IRT for NLP evaluation; leaderboards; annotation error detection via IRT; negative discrimination
summary: Builds a Bayesian IRT leaderboard model in which latent subject skill and item difficulty (and discrimination) predict correct responses, and uses it to analyse ranking reliability, guide annotation, detect overfitting, find informative examples and identify annotation errors.
relation_to_specdx: The direct origin of the 'flag items with negative/low discrimination as annotation errors' heuristic behind B3; it scores responses against a fixed key and gives an untyped flag, while SpecDx keeps the key as one fallible anchor, models which wrong value interpreters produce, and types the defect (contradiction, hidden requirement, ambiguity, weak check).
baseline_notes: B3 reference: fit the 1PL/2PL/IRT-feas models (py-irt implements them) on the binary interpreter × clause pass/fail matrix (subjects = interpreter runs or models, items = clauses or cells; response = 1 if the run's reading/behaviour satisfies the clause or equals the declared value d_c), then rank items by negative or near-zero discrimination as candidate specification defects. Code: the paper's models are in py-irt (nd-ball/py-irt, MIT).

title: Pervasive Label Errors in Test Sets Destabilize Machine Learning Benchmarks
authors: Curtis G. Northcutt; Anish Athalye; Jonas Mueller
venue: Proceedings of the Neural Information Processing Systems Track on Datasets and Benchmarks 1 (NeurIPS 2021)
subtopics: label errors in test sets; confident learning; benchmark instability; human validation
summary: Uses confident learning to flag candidate label errors in the test sets of 10 common vision, language and audio datasets, validates them by crowdsourcing (51% of flags confirmed), estimates at least 3.3% errors on average, and shows that the errors can change which model ranks best.
relation_to_specdx: The canonical demonstration that benchmark 'ground truth' is itself defective, the premise SpecDx extends from labels to executable specifications; detection relies on a trained classifier's probabilities and human confirmation rather than an executor population with witnesses.

title: Item response theory in AI: Analysing machine learning classifiers at the instance level
authors: Fernando Martínez-Plumed; Ricardo B.C. Prudêncio; Adolfo Martínez-Usó; José Hernández-Orallo
venue: Artificial Intelligence
subtopics: instance-level IRT; IRT in machine learning; classifier characteristic curves
summary: Adapts IRT to machine-learning classification by treating instances as items and classifiers as respondents, studies what discrimination, difficulty and guessing mean for instances (and their link to instance hardness), and compares classifiers via classifier characteristic curves.
relation_to_specdx: Foundational instance-level IRT in AI and an early observation that negative-discrimination instances signal noisy or anomalous items; SpecDx's per-cell difficulty β_g plays the same role, but SpecDx adds an explicit fallible anchor, a set-valued truth and an error distribution over wrong values.

title: Learning Latent Parameters without Human Response Patterns: Item Response Theory with Artificial Crowds
authors: John P. Lalor; Hao Wu; Hong Yu
venue: Proceedings of the 2019 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing and the 9th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (EMNLP-IJCNLP)
subtopics: IRT with artificial crowds; machine response patterns
summary: Learns IRT item parameters from response patterns generated by an 'artificial crowd' of DNN models instead of humans, shows medium-to-large correlation with human-derived parameters on NLI and sentiment analysis, and uses learned difficulty for training-set filtering.

title: Building an Evaluation Scale using Item Response Theory
authors: John Lalor; Hao Wu; hong yu
venue: Proceedings of the 2016 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
subtopics: IRT for NLP evaluation; test-set construction; item difficulty/discrimination
summary: Proposes Item Response Theory from psychometrics for building gold-standard NLP test sets: item difficulty and discrimination are estimated from many human responses on a Recognizing Textual Entailment set, and systems are scored against a human ability scale rather than raw accuracy.
relation_to_specdx: Seminal import of IRT into NLP evaluation that SpecDx's σ(α_m − β_g) term and baseline B3 descend from; it treats the gold key as correct and models only respondent ability and item parameters, whereas SpecDx treats the specification's declared value as a fallible anchor with set-valued truth.

title: Estimating Item Parameters and Latent Ability when Responses are Scored in Two or More Nominal Categories
authors: R. Darrell Bock
venue: Psychometrika
subtopics: nominal response model; distractor analysis; information from wrong responses
summary: Proposes the nominal response model, a multivariate logistic latent-trait model giving each response alternative of a multiple-choice item its own parameters, so that information in 'wrong' responses is recovered when estimating ability.
relation_to_specdx: The psychometric ancestor of modelling which wrong value a respondent picks: SpecDx's error distribution over values outside A_c plays the role of the nominal model's distractor curves, and a 'distractor' that attracts high-ability respondents is the classical miskey signal SpecDx generalises to set-valued truth.

title: Adaptive Testing for LLM Evaluation: A Psychometric Alternative to Static Benchmarks
authors: Peiyu Li; Xiuxiu Tang; Si Chen; Ying Cheng; Ronald Metoyer; Ting Hua; Nitesh V Chawla
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (PMLR 306)
subtopics: computerised adaptive testing; IRT for LLM evaluation; Fisher information item selection; negative discrimination
specdx_components: item difficulty/IRT; active synthesis; baseline B3
summary: ATLAS is an IRT-based adaptive testing framework that selects benchmark items by Fisher information, cutting required items by up to 90% (41 HellaSwag items match whole-bank ability with 0.157 MAE) and re-ranking 23–31% of more than 3,000 models by over 10 positions relative to accuracy; code and calibrated item banks are released. Its arXiv version reports that 3–6% of items in five benchmarks show negative discrimination, indicating annotation errors.
relation_to_specdx: Combines two SpecDx ingredients, IRT item calibration from a model population and information-driven item selection (cf. SpecDx's Thompson-sampling scenario synthesis), and reports negative-discrimination items as annotation errors; the goal is ability estimation, not typed defect diagnosis.

title: An Efficient Joint Learning Approach for Item Response Theory
authors: Tanish Agarwal; Kaustubh Shivshankar Shejole; Arpit Agarwal
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (PMLR 306)
subtopics: Rasch model estimation; EM; Pólya-Gamma augmentation; consistency
summary: Proposes an EM algorithm with Pólya-Gamma latent variables for joint estimation of Rasch item and user parameters, theoretically sound and outperforming joint maximum likelihood and the spectral two-step method, especially with few items.
relation_to_specdx: Estimation theory for exactly SpecDx's σ(α_m − β_g) accuracy term with few items or few respondents (SpecDx has few interpreters); it could replace SpecDx's MAP/EM inner step, but it has no anchor, error pool or set-valued truth.

title: How Benchmarks Mis-Score Computer-Use Agents
authors: Zihan Dong; Zhiyuan Ma; Zekun Wang; Yunqing Li; Zirou Liu; Ruixuan Deng; Qishi Zhan; Rui Qian
venue: arXiv
subtopics: computer-use agents; evaluator false negatives; broken tasks; OSWorld/WebArena audit; failure taxonomy
summary: Frames computer-use-agent benchmark scores as outputs of a pipeline (task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, reporting) and audits 150 failure-scored trajectories from five web, enterprise-workflow and desktop benchmarks, finding 15.3% of FAIL verdicts wrong (10.7% evaluator false negatives, 4.7% broken tasks).
relation_to_specdx: Quantifies over-strict checks (evaluator false negatives) and broken tasks in OSWorld-style benchmarks by manual trajectory audit; SpecDx targets the same defect classes automatically and adds the opposite direction (weak checks that pass wrong behaviour). | Quantifies how many agent 'failures' are really check or task defects, motivating SpecDx; the audit is manual.

title: Lost in Benchmarks? Rethinking Large Language Model Benchmarking with Item Response Theory
authors: Hongli Zhou; Hui Huang; Ziqing Zhao; Lvyuan Han; Huicheng Wang; Kehai Chen; Muyun Yang; Wei Bao; Jian Dong; Bing Xu; Conghui Zhu; Hailong Cao; Tiejun Zhao
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
subtopics: IRT for LLM benchmarks; neural IRT; benchmark measurement quality
summary: Proposes PSN-IRT, a pseudo-Siamese neural IRT that estimates model ability and a rich set of item parameters, and uses it to analyse 11 LLM benchmarks (41,871 items), revealing varied measurement-quality shortcomings and enabling smaller benchmarks better aligned with human preference.
relation_to_specdx: A 2026 IRT audit of benchmark item quality from a population of LLMs; it diagnoses measurement properties (difficulty, discrimination, guessing) rather than whether an item's key is wrong, and has no anchor or defect typing.

title: SWE-Bench+: Enhanced LLM Coding Benchmark
authors: Haoran Xue; Reem Aleithan; Nafid Enan; Gias Uddin; Song Wang
venue: Proceedings of the 3rd ACM International Conference on AI-Powered Software
subtopics: SWE-bench data quality; solution leakage; weak tests; benchmark repair; SWE-bench quality; cheating patches
summary: Published version (AIware 2026) of SWE-Bench+ (arXiv 2410.06992): a manual screening of SWE-Agent+GPT-4's successful SWE-bench patches finds 32.67% involve solution leakage (the fix is in the issue text) and 31.08% pass only because of weak tests; filtering them drops the resolution rate from 12.47% to 3.97%, and the same issues appear in SWE-bench Lite and Verified.
relation_to_specdx: Documents the weak-check and leaked-answer problems in the most-used SE agent benchmark by manual inspection; SpecDx's weak-check detection targets the first problem automatically. | Real-world evidence of weak checks and leaky specifications in an agent benchmark, found manually; a source of real defect categories.

title: Measuring what Matters: Construct Validity in Large Language Model Benchmarks
authors: Andrew M. Bean; Ryan Othniel Kearns; Angelika Romanou; Franziska Sofia Hafner; Harry Mayne; Jan Batzner; Negar Foroutan Eghlidi; Chris Schmitz; Karolina Korgul; Hunar Batra; Oishi Deb; Emma Beharry; Cornelius Emde; Thomas Foster; Anna Gausen; María Grandury; Sophia Han; Valentin Hofmann; Lujain Ibrahim; Hazel Kim; Hannah Rose Kirk; Fangru Lin; Gabrielle Liu; Lennart Luettgau; Jabez Magomere; Jonathan Rystrøm; Anna Sotnikova; Yushi Yang; Yilun Zhao; Adel Bibi; Antoine Bosselut; Ronald Clark; Arman Cohan; Jakob Foerster; Yarin Gal; Scott Hale; Deborah Raji; Christopher Summerfield; Philip Torr; Cozmin Ududec; Luc Rocher; Adam Mahdi
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025), Datasets and Benchmarks Track
subtopics: construct validity; systematic review; LLM benchmarks
summary: A systematic review by 29 experts of 445 LLM benchmarks from leading NLP/ML venues, identifying patterns in measured phenomena, tasks and scoring metrics that undermine construct validity, with eight recommendations for benchmark developers.
relation_to_specdx: Establishes construct validity as a recognised failure mode of LLM benchmarks at the benchmark level; SpecDx operates at the item/clause level, checking automatically whether each check C faithfully encodes the stated task T.

title: metabench -- A Sparse Benchmark of Reasoning and Knowledge in Large Language Models
authors: Alex Kipnis; Konstantinos Voudouris; Luca M. Schulze Buschoff; Eric Schulz
venue: The Thirteenth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2025)
subtopics: IRT for LLM evaluation; sparse benchmarks; item informativeness
summary: Uses responses of more than 5000 LLMs to six Open LLM Leaderboard benchmarks (28,632 items) and IRT-based item selection to distil metabench, under 3% of the original size, whose ability estimates reconstruct the original benchmark scores with about 1% RMSE and load on a single common factor.
relation_to_specdx: Large-scale evidence that IRT item parameters can be fitted from a population of LLM respondents; like tinyBenchmarks it optimises measurement efficiency and treats keys as correct, whereas SpecDx targets items whose key is wrong.

title: BetterBench: Assessing AI Benchmarks, Uncovering Issues, and Establishing Best Practices
authors: Anka Reuel; Amelia Hardy; Chandler Smith; Max Lamparth; Malcolm Hardy; Mykel Kochenderfer
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (NeurIPS 2024)
subtopics: benchmark quality assessment; best practices; checklist
summary: Develops an assessment framework of 46 best practices across an AI benchmark's lifecycle, evaluates 24 benchmarks against it, finds large quality differences and common shortcomings, and releases a checklist and living repository.
relation_to_specdx: A lifecycle-level, manual quality checklist for benchmarks; complementary to SpecDx, which automatically diagnoses item-level specification defects.

title: OSWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Open-Ended Tasks in Real Computer Environments
authors: Tianbao Xie; Danyang Zhang; Jixuan Chen; Xiaochuan Li; Siheng Zhao; Ruisheng Cao; Toh Hua; Zhoujun Cheng; Dongchan Shin; Fangyu Lei; Yitao Liu; Yiheng Xu; Shuyan Zhou; Silvio Savarese; Caiming Xiong; Victor Zhong; Tao Yu
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (NeurIPS 2024)
subtopics: computer-use agent benchmark; execution-based evaluation; OSWorld-Verified
summary: OSWorld is a scalable real-computer environment (Ubuntu, Windows, macOS) for multimodal agents with 369 tasks and execution-based evaluation scripts. Its later OSWorld-Verified release (July 2025, announced on the XLANG blog, not a paper) fixed hundreds of broken tasks and evaluators.
relation_to_specdx: An execution-checked benchmark whose evaluation scripts (C) later needed large-scale manual repair; a source of real over-strict and broken-check defects of the kind SpecDx diagnoses.

title: SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-world Github Issues?
authors: Carlos E. Jimenez; John Yang; Alexander Wettig; Shunyu Yao; Kexin Pei; Ofir Press; Karthik Narasimhan
venue: The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2024)
subtopics: SE agent benchmark; issue resolution; test-based checks
summary: SWE-bench is an evaluation framework of 2,294 real GitHub issues and their pull requests from 12 Python repositories; a model must edit the codebase to resolve the issue, and success is judged by the repository's tests, which the best model at the time (Claude 2) passed on 1.96% of issues.
relation_to_specdx: A widely used benchmark whose checks (fail-to-pass tests) were later shown to be weak or wrong (SWE-bench Verified, SWE-Bench+, PatchDiff, SWE-ABS, ABC), giving real weak-check and ambiguity defects of the kind SpecDx diagnoses.

title: tinyBenchmarks: evaluating LLMs with fewer examples
authors: Felipe Maia Polo; Lucas Weber; Leshem Choshen; Yuekai Sun; Gongjun Xu; Mikhail Yurochkin
venue: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (PMLR 235)
subtopics: efficient benchmarking; IRT for LLM evaluation; anchor items; efficient evaluation; IRT; subset selection; LLM benchmarking
summary: Shows that LLM benchmark scores (e.g. MMLU's 14K items) can be estimated from about 100 curated examples, using IRT-based and clustering strategies for item selection and performance estimation, and releases tiny versions of Open LLM Leaderboard, MMLU, HELM and AlpacaEval 2.0 with tools.
relation_to_specdx: Uses IRT fitted on a population of LLMs to pick informative 'anchor' items, which parallels SpecDx's active scenario selection; its goal is cheaper ability estimation assuming correct keys, not finding defective items. | Efficient evaluation by choosing informative items from a fixed pool; SpecDx also economises on executions but generates new scenarios and its estimand is per-cell specification correctness, not model accuracy.

title: CROWDLAB: Supervised learning to infer consensus labels and quality scores for data with multiple annotators
authors: Hui Wen Goh; Ulyana Tkachenko; Jonas Mueller
venue: NeurIPS 2022 Workshop on Human in the Loop Learning
subtopics: multi-annotator consensus; annotator quality; cleanlab
summary: CROWDLAB uses any trained classifier plus a weighted ensemble to estimate a consensus label, a confidence score for it, and a quality rating per annotator for multi-annotator classification data, outperforming generative crowdsourcing models; implemented in cleanlab's multiannotator module.
relation_to_specdx: Gives consensus, per-item confidence and per-annotator quality from a matrix of annotations, structurally like SpecDx's interpreter × cell matrix; but it outputs one consensus label, has no anchor treated as a rater, no set-valued truth and no defect typing.
baseline_notes: cleanlab.multiannotator.get_label_quality_multiannotator(labels_multiannotator, pred_probs): rows = cells, columns = interpreters (model×seed), entries = index of the value read (NaN if unread); add the specification as an extra 'annotator' column holding d_c, and use the population vote distribution as pred_probs. Flag cells where the consensus differs from d_c with high consensus quality (mis-key/hidden requirement); the specification column's annotator-quality score measures overall specification reliability. Offline; cleanlab/cleanlab, Apache-2.0.

title: Detecting Label Errors by Using Pre-Trained Language Models
authors: Derek Chong; Jenny Hong; Christopher Manning
venue: Proceedings of the 2022 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
subtopics: label error detection; pre-trained language models; realistic label noise
summary: Shows that ranking out-of-sample examples by fine-tuned pre-trained LM loss outperforms more complex label-error detectors, and introduces realistic human-originated label noise for SNLI and TweetNLP that is harder to detect than synthetic noise.
relation_to_specdx: Single-model loss ranking is the label-level analogue of baseline B2 (best single interpreter flags all violations); its point that realistic seeded noise beats synthetic noise is relevant to SpecDx's mutation-operator evaluation.

title: AI and the Everything in the Whole Wide World Benchmark
authors: Inioluwa Deborah Raji; Emily M. Bender; Amandalynne Paullada; Emily Denton; Alex Hanna
venue: Proceedings of the Neural Information Processing Systems Track on Datasets and Benchmarks 1 (NeurIPS 2021)
subtopics: construct validity; benchmark critique; position paper
summary: Position paper arguing that influential AI benchmarks are treated as stand-ins for general capability and examining the construct-validity limits of framing them as broad measures of progress.
relation_to_specdx: Frames benchmark validity at the level of what a benchmark measures; SpecDx works at a finer grain, testing whether each check C actually encodes what the stated task T asks (item-level content validity), and does so automatically.

title: Comparing Test Sets with Item Response Theory
authors: Clara Vania; Phu Mon Htut; William Huang; Dhara Mungra; Richard Yuanzhe Pang; Jason Phang; Haokun Liu; Kyunghyun Cho; Samuel R. Bowman
venue: Proceedings of the 59th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics and the 11th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (Volume 1: Long Papers)
subtopics: IRT for NLP evaluation; test-set comparison; saturation
summary: Uses IRT over the per-example predictions of 18 pretrained Transformers on 29 NLU datasets to measure which test sets still discriminate among strong models, finding Quoref, HellaSwag and MC-TACO discriminative and SNLI, MNLI and CommitmentBank saturated.
relation_to_specdx: Shows that a population of models (not humans) suffices to fit IRT item parameters, the same 'artificial crowd' premise as SpecDx's interpreter population; it measures dataset discriminativeness, not item defects, and assumes the gold labels are correct.

title: What Will it Take to Fix Benchmarking in Natural Language Understanding?
authors: Samuel R. Bowman; George Dahl
venue: Proceedings of the 2021 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies
subtopics: benchmark validity; label noise; position paper
summary: Position paper arguing NLU evaluation is broken, laying out four criteria benchmarks should meet, arguing adversarial data collection does not address the causes, and calling for progress in dataset design, annotation reliability, size and handling of social bias.
relation_to_specdx: Names invalid and ambiguously annotated items as a core cause of benchmark failure, the problem SpecDx addresses for executable specifications with automatic detection.

title: Dataset Cartography: Mapping and Diagnosing Datasets with Training Dynamics
authors: Swabha Swayamdipta; Roy Schwartz; Nicholas Lourie; Yizhong Wang; Hannaneh Hajishirzi; Noah A. Smith; Yejin Choi
venue: Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
subtopics: training dynamics; dataset cartography; mislabeled example detection
summary: Introduces data maps built from training dynamics: per-example confidence in the gold class and its variability across epochs, which separate easy-to-learn, ambiguous and hard-to-learn regions; the hard-to-learn region frequently contains labelling errors.
relation_to_specdx: A model-based way to flag suspect gold labels via confidence and variability; it needs gradient training on the dataset, whereas SpecDx reads confidence and variability from a population of off-the-shelf interpreters, a training-free analogue of the confidence × variability plane.

title: Identifying Mislabeled Data using the Area Under the Margin Ranking
authors: Geoff Pleiss; Tianyi Zhang; Ethan R. Elenberg; Kilian Q. Weinberger
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020)
subtopics: training dynamics; mislabeled data; area under the margin; threshold samples
summary: Introduces the Area Under the Margin (AUM) statistic, which exploits differences in training dynamics between clean and mislabeled samples, and learns an AUM threshold by adding an extra class of deliberately mislabeled 'threshold samples'; removing flagged data improves test error on WebVision50 and CIFAR100.
relation_to_specdx: Its threshold-sample trick (calibrate a detector with purposely corrupted items) parallels SpecDx's seeded specification mutations with kill witnesses; AUM needs training a network on the data, which SpecDx avoids.

title: On the Unidentifiability of the Fixed-Effects 3PL Model
authors: Ernesto San Martín; Jorge González; Francis Tuerlinckx
venue: Psychometrika
subtopics: identifiability; 3PL; fixed-effects IRT
summary: Reviews statistical model and parameter identification and their links to interpretability and estimator properties, illustrates them for fixed-effects 1PL, 2PL and 1PL-G models, and proves that item parameters of the fixed-effects 3PL model are not identified and cannot be consistently estimated.
relation_to_specdx: Shows that richer IRT models (e.g. with guessing/ceiling parameters, as in the 4PL-based mislabel indicator) can lose identifiability; SpecDx's identifiability theory (two models with distinct accuracy, or a known error pool) addresses the analogous question for its anchored set-valued model.

title: Bayes Modal Estimation in Item Response Models
authors: Robert J. Mislevy
venue: Psychometrika
subtopics: Bayes modal (MAP) estimation; hierarchical priors; small samples
summary: Presents a Bayesian framework with two-stage priors on item and examinee populations for 1PL/2PL/3PL IRT models and an EM-based procedure for Bayes modal (MAP) point and interval estimation, improving estimation in moderately small samples.
relation_to_specdx: Direct precedent for SpecDx's MAP/EM fitting with priors, which matters because SpecDx has few respondents (local model families) per cell; SpecDx's priors are on the error distribution (Dirichlet around a flat pool) rather than on item parameters only.

title: Developing a Common Metric in Item Response Theory
authors: Martha L. Stocking; Frederic M. Lord
venue: Applied Psychological Measurement
subtopics: IRT linking; anchor items; common metric; equating
summary: Discusses methods for transforming independently estimated IRT item parameters from two data sets onto a common metric (needed for horizontal/vertical equating and item-bias studies) and presents the characteristic-curve linking method now known as Stocking–Lord.
relation_to_specdx: Classical treatment of how anchor (common) items fix the otherwise unidentified location/scale of an IRT metric; SpecDx's anchor is different in kind (the specification's declared value acts as a fallible rater per cell), but the same logic of pinning a latent scale with known reference points underlies its anchor-based contrasts.

title: Marginal Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Item Parameters: Application of an EM Algorithm
authors: R. Darrell Bock; Murray Aitkin
venue: Psychometrika
subtopics: marginal maximum likelihood; EM algorithm; IRT estimation
summary: Shows that marginal maximum likelihood estimation of item parameters, integrating over an empirically characterised ability distribution, becomes practical with an EM algorithm, and that it applies to general (including multidimensional) item response models without simple sufficient statistics.
relation_to_specdx: The EM foundation for latent-trait fitting that SpecDx's MAP/EM fit of interpreter accuracy and cell difficulty builds on; SpecDx's latent variable is the cell's entailment set rather than a continuous ability.

title: Diagnosing the Reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge via Item Response Theory
authors: Junhyuk Choi; Sohhyung Park; Chanhee Cho; Hyeonchu Park; Bugeun Kim
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (PMLR 306)
subtopics: IRT for LLM-as-a-judge; graded response model; measurement reliability
summary: Proposes a two-phase IRT (graded response model) framework for diagnosing LLM-as-a-judge reliability along intrinsic consistency under prompt variation and alignment with human assessments, and applies it to seven LLM judges.
relation_to_specdx: Treats LLMs as measurement instruments whose reliability is estimated with IRT, analogous to SpecDx estimating interpreter accuracy α_m; it audits the judges, not the specification.

title: Understanding Deep Learning Performance through an Examination of Test Set Difficulty: A Psychometric Case Study
authors: John Lalor; Hao Wu; Tsendsuren Munkhdalai; Hong Yu
venue: Proceedings of the 2018 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
subtopics: IRT difficulty; test-set difficulty
summary: Models test-item difficulty with IRT fitted to human response patterns and shows on NLI and sentiment analysis that DNN correctness depends on item difficulty, with easy items learned faster as training data grows.
relation_to_specdx: Supports the premise that item difficulty modulates model correctness (SpecDx's β_g term); it does not address key errors.

title: Identification of Item Response Theory Models
authors: Ernesto San Martín
venue: Handbook of Item Response Theory (Volume 2: Statistical Tools), Chapman and Hall/CRC
subtopics: identifiability; binary IRT models
summary: Handbook chapter on the identification problems of binary IRT models, arguing that each model should be applied to data whose design satisfies the identification restrictions.
relation_to_specdx: Background reference for the identifiability conditions SpecDx states for its anchored cell model.

title: Test Equating, Scaling, and Linking
authors: Michael J. Kolen; Robert L. Brennan
venue: Springer New York (Statistics for Social Science and Behavioral Sciences)
subtopics: test equating; linking; anchor-item designs
summary: Standard reference book on test equating, scaling and linking, covering equating designs with common (anchor) items, IRT linking methods, standard errors of equating and practical issues.
relation_to_specdx: Background for the anchor-item and identifiability vocabulary SpecDx borrows; SpecDx does not equate test forms but uses the declared specification value as an anchor in a truth-inference model.

title: Detecting errors in part-of-speech annotation
authors: Markus Dickinson; W. Detmar Meurers
venue: Proceedings of the Tenth Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (EACL 2003)
subtopics: annotation error detection; variation n-grams; seminal
summary: Seminal method for detecting errors in gold-standard part-of-speech annotation by locating n-grams that occur in the corpus with multiple taggings (variation n-grams), plus closed-class analysis and finite-state tagging guide patterns, illustrated on the Penn Treebank WSJ corpus.
relation_to_specdx: Founding 'inconsistency signals error' idea in AED; SpecDx inverts it, treating consistent deviation of many interpreters from the specification as the defect signal.

title: A Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Detecting and Resolving Pragmatic Ambiguities in Natural Language Requirements
authors: Pavithra PM Nair; Preethu Rose Anish
venue: arXiv
subtopics: pragmatic ambiguity; simulated stakeholders; RAG; LLM population
summary: Detects pragmatic ambiguity in NL requirements by simulating stakeholders of novice, intermediate and expert domain knowledge with retrieval-augmented LLMs and flagging discrepancies between their interpretations; evaluated on two PURE documents with GPT-4o-mini, Mistral-7B, Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B.
relation_to_specdx: Shares the idea of a population of simulated readers whose disagreement signals ambiguity. It compares stated interpretations rather than executed behaviour, has no arbiter C, no model of reader accuracy, and covers only ambiguity.
baseline_notes: Would flag requirement sentences whose interpretations differ across simulated expertise levels. Input: NL requirements plus domain knowledge bases. Adaptation: build novice/expert knowledge bases from the TonomyX knowledge base and τ² docs, run with local models, and compare flagged sentences with SpecDx's ddmin-localised ambiguous sentences; essentially B4 on stated readings instead of behaviour. Code: none linked on the arXiv page.

title: Ambig-SWE: Interactive Agents to Overcome Underspecificity in Software Engineering
authors: Sanidhya Vijayvargiya; Xuhui Zhou; Akhila Yerukola; Maarten Sap; Graham Neubig
venue: The Fourteenth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2026)
subtopics: underspecification; agent benchmarks; SWE-Bench Verified; clarification; SE agents; clarifying questions; SWE-bench
summary: Ambig-SWE is an underspecified variant of SWE-Bench Verified for evaluating whether agents detect underspecificity, ask targeted clarification questions and use the answers; models struggle to distinguish well-specified from underspecified tasks, but interaction improves results by up to 74%.
relation_to_specdx: Seeds underspecification into an agent benchmark derived by human verification, close to SpecDx's seeded-defect evaluation on τ²-style tasks; it tests agents' reactions rather than diagnosing the task specification. | Shows that single agents cannot reliably detect underspecification on their own, which motivates SpecDx's population-level detection; its underspecified SWE-bench variants are seeded 'hidden requirement' defects that could serve as external evaluation material. Accepted at ICLR 2026 according to the arXiv comment.

title: Neurosymbolic Auditing of Natural-Language Software Requirements
authors: Bethel Hall; William Eiers
venue: arXiv
subtopics: ambiguity; inconsistency; SMT; neurosymbolic; sampling variation; medical devices
specdx_components: baseline B1; baseline B4; baseline B5; refutation
summary: VERIMED pairs LLMs with an SMT solver to audit medical-device software requirements: ambiguity is detected from stochastic variation across independent LLM formalisations, and inconsistency, vacuity and safety violations are exposed by solver queries; counterexample feedback raises verified accuracy from 55.4% to 98.5% on a hemodialysis benchmark.
relation_to_specdx: Threatens the novelty claim most directly in this theme: it uses disagreement among several LLM samples as the ambiguity signal and logic (SMT, counterexamples) for inconsistency. Differences: its samples are formalisations of T by one model rather than executions by a multi-family population, there is no accuracy/difficulty model to separate interpreter error from genuine ambiguity, no anchored checks C, and no Hidden-requirement or Weak-check types.
baseline_notes: Would detect ambiguity (variance across k LLM formalisations of each requirement) and inconsistency (SMT unsat) in T. Input: NL requirements. Adaptation: formalise each τ² policy sentence or TonomyX BA statement k times with local models into SMT over the database schema, flag sentences with non-equivalent formalisations as ambiguous, and check C plus formalised T for unsat; this is a strong neurosymbolic static baseline between B1 and B4. Code: none linked on the arXiv page.

title: Underspecification does not imply Incoherence: The Risks of Semantic Collapse in Coding Models
authors: Cedric Richter; Mike Papadakis
venue: arXiv
subtopics: underspecification; semantic collapse; consistent misreading; LLM code generation; incoherence as ambiguity proxy; code generation
specdx_components: identifiability; family effects/correlated errors; anchored cell model; baseline B4
summary: Shows that underspecified task descriptions do not necessarily produce incoherent (divergent) samples: LLMs often collapse onto one coherent but wrong interpretation ('detrimental semantic collapse'), affecting over 10% of MBPP, 3% of HumanEval and 32% of LiveCodeBench tasks, and more than five times as often when underspecification is injected.
relation_to_specdx: Directly relevant to SpecDx's identification assumptions: sampling disagreement alone (ClarifyGPT, SpecFix, VERIMED, B4) misses ambiguity when interpreters collapse, whereas SpecDx also uses consistent deviation from the anchor C (Hidden requirement) and across-family diversity. It also warns that correlated readings can make an agent error look like a spec defect. | Strong evidence that disagreement-only detectors (ClarifyGPT's consistency check, semantic entropy, SpecDx's B4) miss ambiguity when interpreters collapse; SpecDx's anchor d_c and cross-family population are designed to catch exactly this case (consensus that contradicts the specification's checks), so this paper motivates the anchored cell model.

title: Validating Formal Specifications with LLM-Generated Test Cases
authors: Alcino Cunha; Nuno Macedo
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
subtopics: specification validation; LLM-generated tests; Alloy; positive/negative instances; flawed specifications
summary: Empirical study of LLMs (mainly GPT-5) generating positive and negative test cases from NL requirements to validate Alloy formalisations of domain-model structural requirements; the generated tests are largely correct and expose many flawed specifications written by human developers.
relation_to_specdx: Shares SpecDx's T-versus-C setting: NL requirements, an executable/formal specification, and LLM-generated witness instances that a flawed formal specification wrongly accepts (Weak check) or rejects (Hidden requirement). It relies on one LLM's reading as the reference and assumes T is right, whereas SpecDx treats both T and C as fallible and uses a population of interpreters.
baseline_notes: Would detect clauses of C that disagree with T via LLM-generated positive/negative instances. Input: NL requirements plus the formal specification. Adaptation: ask local models to write database states (SQL inserts) that should satisfy or violate each τ²/TonomyX requirement, run C on them, and report clauses that accept negatives (Weak check) or reject positives (Hidden requirement/mis-key); a strong single-reader baseline for SpecDx's T-C defect types. Code: not confirmed.

title: Automated Repair of Ambiguous Problem Descriptions for LLM-Based Code Generation
authors: Haoxiang Jia; Robbie Morris; He Ye; Federica Sarro; Sergey Mechtaev
venue: 2025 40th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)
subtopics: ambiguity; program distribution; testing; specification repair; LLM code generation; ambiguity repair; contrastive specification inference; code generation
specdx_components: baseline B4; set-valued truth; anchored cell model; ddmin
summary: SpecFix treats ambiguity in a problem description as uncertainty in the distribution of programs an LLM generates: it analyses that distribution by testing against the input-output examples, repairs it, and then refines the description by contrastive specification inference so that the LLM's interpretation aligns with the examples; it modifies 43.6% of descriptions and raises Pass@1 on them by 30.9% across four LLMs and three benchmarks.
relation_to_specdx: Threatens the novelty claim for Ambiguity and for 'checks as arbiter': it executes a distribution of sampled interpretations and uses executable examples (a small C) to judge them, then edits T. Differences: interpretations come from one model at a time (no multi-family identification of reader error), the unit is a single function description, defects are not typed (no Contradiction/Hidden requirement/Weak check), there is no MUS/witness reasoning, and the goal is repair for code generation rather than diagnosis of a benchmark specification. | Threatens part of the novelty claim: fully automatic, uses the distribution of LLM interpretations of an NL specification, and anchors it to executable examples (the analogue of SpecDx's checks C) to detect and repair ambiguity. It differs in being single-model, treating the examples as ground truth (SpecDx treats C as a fallible rater and can blame it: hidden requirement, weak check, contradiction), having no executor-reliability model or witnesses, and repairing rather than localising and typing defects.
baseline_notes: Would detect descriptions whose sampled programs disagree or disagree with examples, and propose repaired text. Input: NL description, LLM, input-output examples. Adaptation: treat each τ²/TonomyX scenario as a description with C's expected outcomes as examples; sample several agent runs per scenario with one local model, cluster end states, and flag scenarios with multiple clusters or with clusters inconsistent with C; compare its flagged scenarios with SpecDx's Ambiguity and Hidden-requirement findings. Code: GitHub msv-lab/SpecFix (Python, no licence file, last push 2025-10); uses hosted LLM APIs, swap in Ollama models. | Its detection stage can run on SpecDx inputs: per scenario step, cluster runs by cell values (program-distribution analogue), compare with the declared values d_c (input-output example analogue), and flag steps where the majority cluster disagrees with d_c or where clusters split. Its repair stage (contrastive specification inference) could be compared with SpecDx's ddmin localisation by checking whether the edited sentence is the one SpecDx localises. Code released (msv-lab/SpecFix, Python), designed for HumanEval+/MBPP+; adapting it needs a runner that maps scenario steps to programs.

title: RFCScope: Detecting Logical Ambiguities in Internet Protocol Specifications
authors: Mrigank Pawagi; Lize Shao; Hyeonmin Lee; Yixin Sun; Wenxi Wang
venue: 2025 40th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)
subtopics: protocol specifications; RFC; logical ambiguity; errata study; LLM
specdx_components: baseline B1; defect taxonomy; real-defect benchmark
summary: Studies 11 years of verified technical errata in Standards Track RFCs, identifying seven subtypes of logical ambiguity (including inconsistency and under-specification), and introduces RFCScope, an LLM pipeline with cross-document context, semantic partitioning, bug-type-aware prompts and reasoning-based false-positive filtering; it finds 31 new ambiguities in 14 RFCs, 8 confirmed by authors and 3 accepted as errata.
relation_to_specdx: The most advanced static LLM review of specifications (a strong B1 design: map-reduce over partitions plus validation), with a real-defect taxonomy mined from errata, analogous to SpecDx's real defects from TonomyX history and the τ²-Bench-Verified diff. It never executes the specification or uses checks as arbiter.
baseline_notes: Detects logical ambiguities (inconsistency, under-specification and related subtypes) in long NL specifications. Input: the specification text only. Adaptation: replace RFC cross-document context with the TonomyX knowledge base and tool descriptions, translate bug-type prompts to SpecDx's types, run with local models; this is a published, stronger form of B1. Code: no repository confirmed yet.

title: Automated requirement contradiction detection through formal logic and LLMs
authors: Alexander Elenga Gärtner; Dietmar Göhlich
venue: Automated Software Engineering
subtopics: contradiction detection; formal logic + LLM; controlled natural language
specdx_components: defect taxonomy; baseline B1; baseline B5
summary: ALICE detects and classifies contradictions in requirements written in controlled natural language by combining formal logic with LLMs, guided by an expanded contradiction taxonomy and a seven-question decision tree; it detects 60% of all contradictions and clearly outperforms an LLM-only approach.
relation_to_specdx: Closest NL-requirements counterpart of SpecDx's Contradiction type with logic plus LLMs, but contradictions are sought among requirement statements of T, not as unsatisfiability of executable checks C over behaviours, and nothing is executed or refuted with a witness.
baseline_notes: Would flag pairs of requirement statements in T that contradict each other. Input: requirements in controlled natural language (English). Adaptation: rewrite or translate TonomyX/τ² policy clauses into the CNL; compare its flagged pairs with SpecDx MUS candidates on seeded Contradiction mutants. Code: no public repository found (only the TU Berlin deposit of the paper); would need reimplementation from the paper.

title: CellularLint: A Systematic Approach to Identify Inconsistent Behavior in Cellular Network Specifications
authors: Mirza Masfiqur Rahman; Imtiaz Karim; Elisa Bertino
venue: 33rd USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 24)
subtopics: protocol specifications; 3GPP; inconsistency; LLM; few-shot
summary: CellularLint is a semi-automatic framework that detects inconsistencies in 4G/5G standards using few-shot learning on LLMs domain-adapted to cellular protocol text; on NAS and security specifications it uncovers 157 inconsistencies with 82.67% accuracy, validated on open-source implementations and commercial devices.
relation_to_specdx: A large-scale static LLM detector of contradictions within a standard (B1-style), with impact confirmed on implementations; SpecDx instead finds contradictions among executable checks and confirms them with witnesses, and separates spec defects from interpreter errors.
baseline_notes: Structural analogue; models are domain-adapted to 3GPP text and the pipeline pairs sentences within the standard. Not directly runnable on Vietnamese BA documents.

title: ClarifyGPT: A Framework for Enhancing LLM-Based Code Generation via Requirements Clarification
authors: Fangwen Mu; Lin Shi; Song Wang; Zhuohao Yu; Binquan Zhang; ChenXue Wang; Shichao Liu; Qing Wang
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering
subtopics: ambiguity detection; code consistency check; sampling; clarifying questions; LLM code generation; code generation; execution disagreement
specdx_components: baseline B4; baseline B2; set-valued truth; active synthesis
summary: ClarifyGPT detects whether a code-generation requirement is ambiguous by a code consistency check (sample several programs from the LLM, run them on generated test inputs, and call the requirement ambiguous if their outputs disagree), then asks targeted clarifying questions and regenerates code from the refined requirement.
relation_to_specdx: Threatens the novelty claim for the Ambiguity type: it detects ambiguity by executing several sampled interpretations and measuring behavioural disagreement, which is SpecDx's core signal. Differences: one model's samples (no multi-family population or accuracy model, so model error and genuine ambiguity are conflated), no executable checks C as an arbiter, a single-function requirement rather than a multi-document specification, no localisation within T, and no Contradiction, Hidden-requirement or Weak-check types. | Uses exactly SpecDx's behavioural signal (sampled interpreters of one NL requirement diverge on the same input => the requirement admits several readings) to detect ambiguity automatically. It is single-model, has no anchor (it cannot detect a hidden requirement where all samples agree but disagree with the checks), does not separate agent error from ambiguity, does not localise the ambiguous sentence or type other defects, and resolves ambiguity through a (simulated) user.
baseline_notes: Would flag a scenario/requirement as ambiguous when sampled executions disagree. Input: a requirement, an LLM, and inputs to execute on. Adaptation: per scenario, sample k runs of one local model on the τ²/TonomyX task and flag cells whose end-state values disagree; this is essentially B4 restricted to one family and without C, a natural ablation of SpecDx. Code: GitHub ClarifyGPT/ClarifyGPT (Python, no licence file, last push 2023-10; linked from the paper's references); built for OpenAI APIs. | Most direct baseline for SpecDx's ambiguity type. Adaptation: for each scenario step, treat the runs of one model (seeds x Tell variants) as ClarifyGPT's n sampled programs and the scenario's database state as the test input; the requirement is ambiguous if the runs' cell values are not all identical (ClarifyGPT's rule), optionally with a threshold on the number of distinct clusters to tolerate agent noise. Pooling models gives a multi-family variant. Inputs: the run matrix only. Output: per-step/per-cell ambiguity flag, no defect typing. No official code release found (FSE artifact not located); the detector is a few lines to reimplement.

title: Translation Titans, Reasoning Challenges: Satisfiability-Aided Language Models for Detecting Conflicting Requirements
authors: Mohamad Fazelnia; Mehdi Mirakhorli; Hamid Bagheri
venue: Proceedings of the 39th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering
subtopics: conflict detection; SMT; LLM; neurosymbolic; conflicting requirements; LLM + SMT
summary: SAT-LLM has an LLM translate NL requirements into SMT constraints and an SMT solver decide conflicts, outperforming ChatGPT-only conflict detection in early experiments.
relation_to_specdx: Shares the LLM-plus-solver pattern for contradictions; SpecDx avoids relying on one LLM's formalisation of T: contradictions are found among the already-executable clauses C from sampled correction sets, and candidates are refuted by witness states. | LLM + solver for requirement conflicts, i.e. a combination of LLM and logic for specification defects. It uses one LLM as a translator and the solver for consistency only; SpecDx uses a population of LLM executors as statistical evidence and covers four defect types with witnesses.
baseline_notes: Would detect conflicts among requirement statements after LLM translation to SMT. Input: NL requirements. Adaptation: run with a local LLM (Ollama) on τ² policy text and TonomyX BA statements, solve with Z3, and compare with SpecDx Contradiction findings; doubles as a B5-style symbolic baseline. Code: none found; reimplementation from the NIER paper is simple (prompt + Z3).

title: Inconsistency Detection in Natural Language Requirements using ChatGPT: a Preliminary Evaluation
authors: Alessandro Fantechi; Stefania Gnesi; Lucia Passaro; Laura Semini
venue: 2023 IEEE 31st International Requirements Engineering Conference (RE)
subtopics: inconsistency; ChatGPT; LLM
summary: Measures how well GPT-3.5 detects inconsistency defects in NL requirements, comparing its output with expert judgements on a few example requirements documents; early experiments indicate it finds inconsistencies that traditional NLP tools miss.
relation_to_specdx: The earliest direct form of B1 (static LLM review for contradictions). SpecDx's Contradiction is defined by unsatisfiability of C over behaviours and is confirmed by MUS candidates and witness-based refutation, not by an LLM's judgement on text.

title: nl2spec: Interactively Translating Unstructured Natural Language to Temporal Logics with Large Language Models
authors: Matthias Cosler; Christopher Hahn; Daniel Mendoza; Frederik Schmitt; Caroline Trippel
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
subtopics: NL to temporal logic; LLM; ambiguity resolution; sub-translations
summary: nl2spec uses LLMs to translate unstructured natural language into temporal-logic formulas and detects and resolves ambiguity by mapping subformulas back to NL fragments, which users interactively add, delete or edit.
relation_to_specdx: A structural analogue: ambiguity is localised to NL fragments through their formal sub-translations. SpecDx localises ambiguous sentences of T automatically (ddmin with an LLM-population oracle) and judges readings by C, with no human in the loop.
baseline_notes: Would expose ambiguity as alternative sub-translations of each NL fragment. Input: short NL requirements and an LLM. Adaptation: change the target logic from LTL to SQL predicates over the TonomyX schema, sample several translations per τ² policy sentence with local models, and flag sentences with conflicting sub-translations; interactive step must be automated. Code: GitHub realChrisHahn2/nl2spec (MIT, Python; last push 2024).

title: Capture, Analyze, Diagnose: Realizability Checking Of Requirements in FRET
authors: Andreas Katis; Anastasia Mavridou; Dimitra Giannakopoulou; Thomas Pressburger; Johann Schumann
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
subtopics: realizability; conflict diagnosis; counterexamples; FRET
summary: Presents FRET's realizability analysis framework for formalised requirements, with state-of-the-art algorithms over infinite theories and a diagnosis process that visualises conflicts between requirements and simulates counterexamples, applied to industrial case studies.
relation_to_specdx: Conflict diagnosis by minimal conflicting requirement sets plus counterexamples is the formal counterpart of SpecDx's MUS candidates and witness refutation; SpecDx obtains candidates from sampled behaviours of LLM executors over database clauses rather than from temporal-logic requirements, and must also separate executor error.

title: Semi-automated protocol disambiguation and code generation
authors: Jane Yen; Tamás Lévai; Qinyuan Ye; Xiang Ren; Ramesh Govindan; Barath Raghavan
venue: Proceedings of the 2021 ACM SIGCOMM 2021 Conference
subtopics: protocol specifications; RFC; ambiguity; under-specification; code generation; CCG parsing; specification ambiguity; semantic parsing
summary: Sage parses RFC text with a CCG semantic parser and flags sentences with multiple logical forms (ambiguous) or that fail unit tests after code generation (under-specified); after the author clarifies them, it generates protocol code. On the ICMP RFC it finds 5 ambiguous and 6 under-specified sentences and then generates code interoperable with Linux.
relation_to_specdx: The strongest structural analogue: ambiguity = several readings of a sentence, under-specification exposed by executing generated code against tests, and sentence-level localisation. Sage uses one symbolic parser (readings = parses) and a human to resolve; SpecDx uses a population of LLM executors as readers, C as the test oracle, a statistical model to separate reader error, and automatic ddmin localisation. | Localises ambiguity to individual sentences of a natural-language specification by counting readings, as SpecDx's ddmin localisation does with an LLM-population oracle; Sage uses a semantic parser and human clarification rather than behavioural evidence and checks.
