summary: Staccato is a low-cost approximate minimal hitting set algorithm that orders elements by a spectrum-based (SFL) statistical heuristic and can stop early with a partial set of approximately minimal hitting sets; orders of magnitude faster than brute force while capturing the important solutions, scaling to millions of variables.
relation_to_specdx: Statistics-guided approximate hitting sets are the nearest prior art to SpecDx's "soft" minimal hitting sets; Staccato prunes by suspiciousness but still treats every failing observation as a hard set to hit.

title: A practical evaluation of spectrum-based fault localization
authors: Rui Abreu; Peter Zoeteweij; Rob Golsteijn; Arjan J.C. van Gemund
venue: Journal of Systems and Software
subtopics: spectrum-based fault localisation; evaluation; test design
summary: Evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of SFL, which rests on statistical coincidences between failures and component activity, on the Siemens set and the space program as a function of spectrum quality and quantity, parameters that relate to test design.
relation_to_specdx: Standard reference for SFL accuracy limits; SpecDx must beat this kind of statistical coincidence analysis on its interpreter x clause spectra.

title: Diagnosing Multiple Persistent and Intermittent Faults
authors: Johan de Kleer
venue: Proceedings of the 21st International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI 2009)
subtopics: model-based diagnosis; intermittent faults; probe selection
summary: Extends model-based diagnosis, which usually presumes non-intermittent behaviour over few time instants, to intermittent failures observed over time, and shows where to insert probes to isolate the faults that best explain the symptoms at minimum expected cost.
relation_to_specdx: Intermittent faults make the same component fail in some observations but not others, as a specification defect shows up in some interpreter runs but not all; SpecDx models this through interpreter accuracy rather than component intermittency.

title: Finding All Justifications of OWL DL Entailments
authors: Aditya Kalyanpur; Bijan Parsia; Matthew Horridge; Evren Sirin
venue: The Semantic Web: ISWC 2007 + ASWC 2007 (LNCS 4825)
subtopics: ontology debugging; justifications; MUS enumeration
summary: Presents algorithms that compute all justifications (minimal axiom sets sufficient for an entailment) of OWL-DL entailments, essential for debugging unsatisfiable classes and contradictions, and shows that a reasoner-independent hitting-set approach works well on real ontologies.
relation_to_specdx: Justification enumeration via Reiter-style hitting-set trees is MUS enumeration for knowledge bases; SpecDx enumerates the analogous minimal clause sets but from sampled behaviour, not from a reasoner.

title: On the Accuracy of Spectrum-based Fault Localization
authors: Rui Abreu; Peter Zoeteweij; Arjan J.C. van Gemund
venue: Testing for DR: Academic and Industrial Conference Practice and Research Techniques - MUTATION (TAICPART-MUTATION 2007)
subtopics: spectrum-based fault localisation; Ochiai; observation quality
summary: Studies the diagnostic accuracy of spectrum-based fault localisation on the Siemens set as a function of the quality and quantity of spectra and error observations; the Ochiai coefficient is consistently best, and near-optimal accuracy is reached even with low-quality error observations and few tests.
relation_to_specdx: Early evidence that spectrum statistics tolerate poor-quality (noisy) error observations, relevant to SpecDx's noisy interpreter verdicts; Ochiai on the interpreter x clause matrix is the simplest B3-like baseline.

title: HDD: hierarchical delta debugging
authors: Ghassan Misherghi; Zhendong Su
venue: Proceedings of the 28th international conference on Software engineering
subtopics: hierarchical delta debugging; tree-structured input
summary: HDD applies delta debugging level by level to tree-structured inputs (e.g. XML), from coarse to fine, so all candidates stay syntactically valid; it produces simpler outputs with orders of magnitude fewer tests than flat ddmin.
relation_to_specdx: A specification T is hierarchical (document, section, clause, sentence); HDD-style reduction would cut SpecDx's oracle calls.

title: Empirical evaluation of the tarantula automatic fault-localization technique
authors: James A. Jones; Mary Jean Harrold
venue: Proceedings of the 20th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering
subtopics: Tarantula; spectrum-based fault localisation; empirical evaluation
summary: Compares the Tarantula fault-localisation technique with four other techniques on the same subjects; Tarantula is consistently more effective and comparable in cost to the most efficient techniques.
relation_to_specdx: Tarantula is the canonical suspiciousness metric; on SpecDx's interpreter x clause matrix it is a naive baseline that cannot separate agent errors from specification defects.

title: Scalable statistical bug isolation
authors: Ben Liblit; Mayur Naik; Alice X. Zheng; Alex Aiken; Michael I. Jordan
venue: Proceedings of PLDI 2005 (ACM SIGPLAN Notices 40(6))
subtopics: statistical debugging; cooperative bug isolation; multiple bugs
summary: Statistical debugging algorithm that isolates multiple undiagnosed bugs from sampled predicate data of many runs, separating the effects of different bugs and finding predictors associated with each.
relation_to_specdx: Statistics over a population of (user) runs to separate several causes of failure, analogous to SpecDx separating specification defects from scattered agent errors; Liblit et al. localise code predicates and assume a correct failure oracle.

title: Yesterday, my program worked. Today, it does not. Why?
authors: Andreas Zeller
venue: ESEC/FSE 1999 (ACM SIGSOFT Software Engineering Notes 24(6))
subtopics: delta debugging; failure-inducing changes
summary: Introduces delta debugging: given a working "yesterday" version and a failing "today" version, an efficient algorithm isolates a minimal set of failure-inducing changes by systematically testing subsets.
relation_to_specdx: Origin of the ddmin family that SpecDx uses to localise ambiguity among the sentences of T.

title: Identifying the Minimal Transversals of a Hypergraph and Related Problems
authors: Thomas Eiter; Georg Gottlob
venue: SIAM Journal on Computing
subtopics: hypergraph transversals; duality; complexity
summary: Studies hypergraph saturation and recognition of the transversal hypergraph, relates them to many search problems in computer science (including model-based diagnosis and minimal keys), and analyses their complexity.
relation_to_specdx: Complexity foundation of the minimal-hitting-set/transversal problem that SpecDx's MUS-candidate step must solve.

title: Characterizing diagnoses and systems
authors: Johan de Kleer; Alan K. Mackworth; Raymond Reiter
venue: Artificial Intelligence
subtopics: kernel diagnoses; prime implicants; diagnosis theory
summary: Analyses the concept of diagnosis with (prime) implicates and implicants, shows that minimal diagnoses are inadequate in general because supersets of a diagnosis need not be diagnoses, and introduces kernel diagnoses, valid for both consistency-based and abductive views.
relation_to_specdx: Clarifies when minimal hitting sets characterise all diagnoses; relevant because SpecDx's violated-clause sets need not be upward closed.

title: Using crude probability estimates to guide diagnosis
authors: Johan de Kleer
venue: Artificial Intelligence
subtopics: probabilistic diagnosis; fault probabilities; focusing
summary: Shows how crude (order-of-magnitude) prior failure probabilities of components can focus model-based diagnosis on the most probable candidates; the approach generalises to partitions of components with equal failure probability (abstract not available to us beyond this).
relation_to_specdx: Probability-guided focusing on likely diagnoses, analogous to SpecDx ranking soft hitting sets by posterior weight.

title: A correction to the algorithm in reiter's theory of diagnosis
authors: Russell Greiner; Barbara A. Smith; Ralph W. Wilkerson
venue: Artificial Intelligence
subtopics: HS-tree; HS-DAG; diagnosis algorithm correction
summary: Shows that Reiter's hitting-set-tree algorithm can miss diagnoses under certain conditions and presents a corrected algorithm (the HS-DAG) with a proof of correctness.
relation_to_specdx: The corrected hitting-set procedure that any exact implementation of SpecDx's step 3 should follow.

title: Input Reduction Enhanced LLM-based Program Repair
authors: Boyang Yang; Luyao Ren; Xin Yin; Jiadong Ren; Haoye Tian; Shunfu Jin
venue: arXiv
subtopics: input reduction; LLM program repair; ReduceFix
summary: ReduceFix prompts an LLM to generate a reducer that minimises failure-inducing test inputs and feeds the reduced inputs to LLM-based program repair, improving pass@10 on a new long-input benchmark (LFTBench).
relation_to_specdx: Reduction to fight long-context degradation of LLMs; relevant only as LLM-era input reduction.

title: Validity-Preserving Delta Debugging via Generator Trace Reduction
authors: Luyao Ren; Xing Zhang; Ziyue Hua; Yanyan Jiang; Xiao He; Yingfei Xiong; Tao Xie
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
subtopics: validity-preserving delta debugging; generator traces
summary: GReduce reduces bug-inducing inputs by searching over executions of the input generator, so that reduced inputs remain valid with respect to specifications beyond syntax.
relation_to_specdx: Validity-preserving reduction; SpecDx's reduced T must stay a readable specification, a validity constraint of the same kind.

title: A Probabilistic Delta Debugging Approach for Abstract Syntax Trees
authors: Guancheng Wang; Yiqian Wu; Qihao Zhu; Yingfei Xiong; Xin Zhang; Lu Zhang
venue: 2023 IEEE 34th International Symposium on Software Reliability Engineering (ISSRE)
subtopics: probabilistic delta debugging; AST reduction
summary: Integrates ProbDD's probabilistic model into AST-based, domain-specific delta debugging (Perses-style), improving efficiency and effectiveness of program minimisation.
relation_to_specdx: ProbDD follow-up for hierarchical inputs; relevant if T is reduced hierarchically (document > section > sentence).

title: Debugging Flaky Tests using Spectrum-based Fault Localization
authors: Martin Gruber; Gordon Fraser
venue: 2023 IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automation of Software Test (AST)
subtopics: flaky tests; spectrum-based fault localisation
summary: SFFL extends coverage-based SFL to locate the root causes of flaky tests, exploiting the observation that most flaky tests show varying coverage across runs and distinguishing stable from flaky coverage.
relation_to_specdx: Uses run-to-run variation of spectra as signal, as SpecDx uses interpreter-to-interpreter variation.

title: Logical bytecode reduction
authors: Christian Gram Kalhauge; Jens Palsberg
venue: Proceedings of the 42nd ACM SIGPLAN International Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation
subtopics: logical reduction; propositional dependencies; bytecode
summary: Specifies valid sub-inputs with a propositional formula over fine-grained dependencies and runs a reduction algorithm that finds a small, valid, failure-inducing input, giving much more reduction than J-Reduce on Java bytecode.
relation_to_specdx: Validity-preserving reduction via logic; relevant if reduced versions of T must stay well-formed.

title: On the Impact of Flaky Tests in Automated Program Repair
authors: Yihao Qin; Shangwen Wang; Kui Liu; Xiaoguang Mao; Tegawende F. Bissyande
venue: 2021 IEEE International Conference on Software Analysis, Evolution and Reengineering (SANER)
subtopics: flaky tests; program repair; fault localisation
summary: Reintroduces flaky tests into Defects4J and shows that although they are few they affect most bugs and drastically hinder spectrum-based fault localisation and automated program repair.
relation_to_specdx: Evidence that SFL breaks under even small amounts of outcome noise, as in SpecDx's noisy behavioural spectra.

title: Test Case Reduction: A Framework, Benchmark, and Comparative Study
authors: Patrick Kreutzer; Tom Kunze; Michael Philippsen
venue: 2021 IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME)
subtopics: test-case reduction; benchmark; comparative study
summary: Provides a framework with tuned implementations of six language-agnostic reducers, a benchmark of 321 bug-inducing programs in two languages (110 real compiler bugs), and a comparative study finding that no reducer is best across all cases.
relation_to_specdx: Methodological model for comparing ddmin variants (ddmin vs ProbDD/CDD) in SpecDx's ambiguity-localisation ablation.

title: Group Testing: An Information Theory Perspective
authors: Matthew Aldridge; Oliver Johnson; Jonathan Scarlett
venue: Foundations and Trends in Communications and Information Theory (now publishers)
subtopics: group testing; noisy group testing; sparse inference
summary: Monograph surveying group testing (identifying a few defective items from tests on pools, positive if a pool contains a defective) from an information-theoretic view: practical algorithms, achievability and converse bounds, including noisy test models.
relation_to_specdx: Group testing with noisy tests is the information-theoretic cousin of SpecDx's problem (which clauses are defective, from noisy pooled pass/fail behaviour); its bounds could inform how many interpreter runs are needed.

title: Perses: syntax-guided program reduction
authors: Chengnian Sun; Yuanbo Li; Qirun Zhang; Tianxiao Gu; Zhendong Su
venue: Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Software Engineering
subtopics: program reduction; syntax-guided; Perses
summary: Perses performs syntax-guided program reduction, using the formal grammar so that every reduction step considers only smaller, syntactically valid variants, outperforming DD, HDD and C-Reduce in speed and output size while remaining language-general.
relation_to_specdx: Validity-aware reduction framework; the uw-pluverse/perses repository also hosts later reducers from the same group.

title: Coarse Hierarchical Delta Debugging
authors: Renata Hodovan; Akos Kiss; Tibor Gyimothy
venue: 2017 IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME)
subtopics: hierarchical delta debugging; coarse HDD; picireny
summary: Proposes Coarse HDD, a variant of hierarchical delta debugging for tree-structured (grammar-parsed) inputs; the authors maintain the picireny HDD framework (abstract not read; summary from the publication record and tool description).
relation_to_specdx: picireny/picire (by the same authors) are maintained Python ddmin/HDD frameworks that SpecDx could reuse for sentence- or section-level reduction of T with a custom population oracle.

title: Parallelized Hitting Set Computation for Model-Based Diagnosis
authors: Dietmar Jannach; Thomas Schmitz; Kostyantyn Shchekotykhin
venue: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
subtopics: HS-tree; parallel diagnosis
summary: Parallelises the construction of Reiter's breadth-first hitting-set tree on multi-core CPUs without losing diagnoses, significantly reducing running times on benchmark problems, and studies how problem structure affects the gains.
relation_to_specdx: Engineering option for exact hitting-set enumeration if SpecDx's candidate step becomes a bottleneck.

title: A feedback technique for unsatisfiable UML/OCL class diagrams
authors: Asadullah Shaikh; Uffe Kock Wiil
venue: Software: Practice and Experience
subtopics: UML/OCL; unsatisfiability feedback; model slicing
summary: Feedback technique that slices a UML/OCL class diagram into submodels, detects unsatisfiable submodels and reports the integrity constraints responsible, so developers can focus on the faulty part of the model.
relation_to_specdx: Unsatisfiable-core feedback for a declarative data model with integrity constraints, close to SpecDx's database invariants; it is purely symbolic and finds only contradictions.

title: Test-case reduction for C compiler bugs
authors: John Regehr; Yang Chen; Pascal Cuoq; Eric Eide; Chucky Ellison; Xuejun Yang
venue: Proceedings of the 33rd ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation
subtopics: test-case reduction; C-Reduce; compiler testing
summary: Presents C-Reduce and related domain-specific reducers that go beyond substring-removing delta debugging by applying C-aware transformations, producing much smaller compiler-bug test cases while avoiding undefined behaviour.
relation_to_specdx: Shows the value of domain-aware reduction transformations; SpecDx's sentence-level ddmin over T is generic and could in principle use semantics-aware transformations of requirement text.

title: Sequential Diagnosis by Abstraction
authors: S. A. Siddiqi; J. Huang
venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research
subtopics: sequential diagnosis; measurement selection; abstraction
summary: Sequential diagnosis framework that chooses measurement points with an efficiently computed heuristic not requiring the full set of diagnoses, plus abstraction techniques, scaling entropy-style measurement selection to much larger systems.
relation_to_specdx: Scalable next-measurement selection, related to SpecDx's choice of the next scenario.

title: Automated diagnosis of feature model configurations
authors: J. White; D. Benavides; D.C. Schmidt; P. Trinidad; B. Dougherty; A. Ruiz-Cortes
venue: Journal of Systems and Software
subtopics: feature models; configuration diagnosis; CSP
summary: Transforms feature models and invalid product-line configurations into constraint satisfaction problems to automatically diagnose configuration errors and propose minimal repairs of feature selections (the CURE approach).
relation_to_specdx: Diagnosis of a configuration against a variability specification by CSP; SpecDx diagnoses the specification itself rather than a configuration.

title: Plausible Repairs for Inconsistent Requirements
authors: Alexander Felfernig; Gerhard Friedrich; Monika Schubert; Monika Mandl; Markus Mairitsch; Erich Teppan
venue: Proceedings of the 21st International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI 2009)
subtopics: inconsistent requirements; personalised diagnosis; collaborative filtering
summary: For knowledge-based recommenders whose user requirements admit no recommendation, integrates the computation of minimal faulty-requirement explanations with collaborative problem solving to propose personalised, plausible repairs.
relation_to_specdx: Uses population (collaborative) data to rank diagnoses of an inconsistent requirement set, a distant analogue of SpecDx's population statistics; the requirements are user preferences, not a specification.

title: Diagnosis of discrete-event systems from uncertain temporal observations
authors: Gianfranco Lamperti; Marina Zanella
venue: Artificial Intelligence
subtopics: discrete-event systems; uncertain observations; diagnosis
summary: Diagnosis of discrete-event (active) systems when the observation channel may add spurious messages, lose messages or lose temporal ordering, so observations are uncertain and underconstrained; illustrated on power transmission networks.
relation_to_specdx: An early treatment of corrupted observations in diagnosis; SpecDx's observations are corrupted by interpreter errors rather than a lossy channel.

title: When Agents Disagree With Themselves: Behavioral Consistency as an Uncertainty Signal for LLM Agents
authors: Aman Mehta
venue: arXiv
subtopics: behavioural consistency; agents; sampling-based uncertainty
summary: Runs the same LLM agent repeatedly on identical inputs and uses the number of distinct action sequences as a training-free uncertainty signal; on HotpotQA (8,000 runs, four models) and SWE-bench, consistent tasks are far more accurate, divergence concentrates at early steps, and agreement-based selective prediction matches split-conformal baselines.
relation_to_specdx: Uses the variance of agent trajectories across repeated runs as a signal, as SpecDx does with its run populations; it attributes divergence to task difficulty/agent uncertainty, while SpecDx localises divergence to cells and steps and separates specification defects from agent errors.
baseline_notes: Per scenario step, count distinct action sequences (or distinct cell values) across seeds of one model, then average over models; flag steps with many distinct paths. Trivial to reimplement on SpecDx run logs; ICML 2026 workshop preprint, no code link found.

title: Correlated Errors in Large Language Models
authors: Elliot Myunghoon Kim; Avi Garg; Kenny Peng; Nikhil Garg
venue: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025)
subtopics: correlated errors; LLM homogeneity; monoculture; LLM-as-judge; correlated LLM errors; algorithmic monoculture
summary: Evaluates more than 350 LLMs on two leaderboards and a resume-screening task and finds strongly correlated errors (models agree 60% of the time when both err); shared architecture and provider drive correlation, but larger, more accurate models are highly correlated even across providers, with consequences for LLM-as-judge and hiring.
relation_to_specdx: Direct empirical challenge to SpecDx's assumption that errors are independent across model families: consensus deviations may reflect shared model biases rather than specification defects. SpecDx should cite it, measure within/across-family error correlation on its populations, and rely on anchor contrasts and refutation witnesses rather than consensus alone. | It is direct empirical evidence against SpecDx's cross-family independence assumption, and especially strong for capable models. SpecDx must quantify residual cross-family correlation, e.g. by a CAPA-style statistic on its matrix, and show that its defect calls survive it.

title: Great Models Think Alike and this Undermines AI Oversight
authors: Shashwat Goel; Joschka Strüber; Ilze Amanda Auzina; Karuna K Chandra; Ponnurangam Kumaraguru; Douwe Kiela; Ameya Prabhu; Matthias Bethge; Jonas Geiping
venue: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025)
subtopics: model similarity; correlated errors; CAPA; AI oversight; LLM-as-judge bias
specdx_components: family effects/correlated errors; identifiability; baseline B4
summary: Proposes CAPA (Chance Adjusted Probabilistic Agreement), a metric of LM similarity based on overlap in mistakes; shows that LLM judges favour similar models, weak-to-strong gains are larger for dissimilar models, and model mistakes become more similar as capability grows.
relation_to_specdx: CAPA is a ready metric for quantifying error correlation between SpecDx's model families, which its identifiability theory assumes away; the finding that stronger models err more alike suggests that SpecDx's accuracy-gradient signatures must account for capability-dependent correlation. | CAPA is a ready-made statistic for SpecDx's family effects: compute it between interpreters on clause outcomes to check the independence assumption and to weight families. It is also a reminder that a committee of similar models over-agrees.
baseline_notes: Use CAPA as a diagnostic of the independence assumption on SpecDx populations, not as a defect detector.

title: HumanEvalComm: Benchmarking the Communication Competence of Code Generation for LLMs and LLM Agent
authors: Jie Jw Wu; Fatemeh H. Fard
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
subtopics: code generation; clarifying questions; ambiguity; inconsistency; incompleteness; benchmark; LLM agents
summary: Builds HumanEvalComm by modifying HumanEval problem descriptions to be ambiguous, inconsistent or incomplete, and measures whether code LLMs and an LLM agent (Okanagan) ask clarifying questions instead of coding; most models rarely ask questions even when the requirement is defective.
relation_to_specdx: Seeds requirement defects (ambiguity, inconsistency, incompleteness) into specifications, which mirrors SpecDx's specification mutation operators and its defect taxonomy; HumanEvalComm evaluates individual models' communication, whereas SpecDx uses many fallible executors to detect and type the seeded defect, and its mutated problems could serve as an external evaluation set. | Builds seeded requirement defects (ambiguity, inconsistency, incompleteness) by mutating problem statements, which parallels SpecDx's mutation operators; it evaluates interpreters' reactions to defects rather than diagnosing the defects.

title: Stress-Testing Model Specs Reveals Character Differences among Language Models
authors: Jifan Zhang; Henry Sleight; Andi Peng; John Schulman; Esin Durmus
venue: arXiv
subtopics: specification stress-testing; cross-model disagreement; model specs; contradiction; ambiguity
specdx_components: baseline B4; family effects/correlated errors; defect taxonomy
summary: Stress-tests AI model specifications by generating value-tradeoff scenarios that pit pairs of principles against each other, collecting responses from twelve frontier LLMs, and measuring behavioural disagreement; high cross-model divergence (over 70,000 cases) is shown to predict specification problems such as direct contradictions and interpretive ambiguities.
relation_to_specdx: Closest in spirit: cross-model behavioural disagreement used to find contradictions and ambiguities in a natural-language specification. It differs in that the specification has no executable checks (no anchor), disagreement is the only signal (no latent executor-accuracy model, no hidden-requirement or weak-check types), diagnosis is qualitative rather than localised with witnesses, and it targets value principles rather than business specifications.
baseline_notes: Its pipeline is essentially B4 with scenario generation: generate scenarios, run several model families, score each response on a classification rubric, and flag scenarios with high inter-model divergence. On SpecDx: use the same run populations, compute per-cell divergence across families, and rank cells; the comparison shows what the anchor, the latent model and MUS refutation add. No code release found.

title: Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy
authors: Sebastian Farquhar; Jannik Kossen; Lorenz Kuhn; Yarin Gal
venue: Nature
subtopics: sampling-based uncertainty; semantic entropy; hallucination detection
summary: Uses semantic entropy, computed over entailment-based clusters of sampled answers, to detect confabulations (arbitrary, incorrect generations) of LLMs across datasets and domains without task-specific data, extending it to longer passages by decomposing them into factual claims.
relation_to_specdx: The main published, code-backed form of the entropy-of-meanings signal that SpecDx's B4 baseline uses; it diagnoses the model's own uncertainty, whereas SpecDx attributes cross-family disagreement to the specification versus the executors.
baseline_notes: Same adaptation as the ICLR 2023 semantic entropy paper; the jlko/semantic_uncertainty implementation includes the entailment clustering and discrete semantic entropy (works on sampled strings only, so it applies to runs from local Ollama models without logits).

title: Generating with Confidence: Uncertainty Quantification for Black-box Large Language Models
authors: Zhen Lin; Shubhendu Trivedi; Jimeng Sun
venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research
subtopics: sampling-based uncertainty; black-box UQ; semantic dispersion
summary: Studies uncertainty quantification for black-box LLM generation, distinguishes uncertainty (dispersion of possible outputs) from confidence (in a given output), and proposes similarity-graph measures (e.g. number of semantic sets, eigenvalue-based dispersion, degree) for selective generation; simple semantic-dispersion measures predict response quality well.
relation_to_specdx: Its graph-based dispersion measures over sampled outputs are drop-in disagreement statistics for SpecDx's B4; like semantic entropy, they measure a model's uncertainty, not whether a specification's declared value is defective.
baseline_notes: Per cell, build a similarity graph over the runs' readings (exact match or NLI for text), compute U_EigV / U_Deg / U_Ecc dispersion; per-run confidence C_Deg of the anchor value d_c gives an anchored variant. Code is MIT, black-box, and works offline with a local NLI model.

title: LLM-Based Test-Driven Interactive Code Generation: User Study and Empirical Evaluation
authors: Sarah Fakhoury; Aaditya Naik; Georgios Sakkas; Saikat Chakraborty; Shuvendu K. Lahiri
venue: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering
subtopics: code generation; intent clarification; tests as specification; intent formalisation; tests as partial specifications; interactive clarification
summary: Proposes TiCoder, an interactive workflow in which an LLM generates candidate code and tests, the user approves or rejects tests to partially formalise intent, and code suggestions are pruned and ranked accordingly; a 15-programmer user study and benchmark evaluation show large gains in pass@1 with few interactions.
relation_to_specdx: Uses tests that discriminate among sampled program interpretations to resolve NL intent ambiguity, which parallels SpecDx's active scenario synthesis that chooses scenarios to maximise information about latent readings; TiCoder needs a human oracle and targets code suggestions, whereas SpecDx is fully automatic and diagnoses defects in the specification itself, including its checks. | Uses executable tests to disambiguate NL intent, choosing tests that discriminate between candidate programs, akin to SpecDx's information-gain scenario synthesis; it relies on a user as the arbiter rather than checks C.
baseline_notes: Requires a user to answer test-approval queries; could only be run with an LLM-simulated user, which collapses into an LLM-population oracle.

title: Nuances are the Key: Unlocking ChatGPT to Find Failure-Inducing Tests with Differential Prompting
authors: Tsz-On Li; Wenxi Zong; Yibo Wang; Haoye Tian; Ying Wang; Shing-Chi Cheung; Jeff Kramer
venue: 2023 38th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)
subtopics: differential testing; LLM test generation; program intention inference
summary: Shows that ChatGPT rarely finds failure-inducing tests directly (28.8%) and proposes Differential Prompting: the LLM infers the intended behaviour of a buggy program, synthesises several reference versions, and tests inputs on which the versions and the program under test disagree; it reaches about 75% success on QuixBugs and 66.7% on Codeforces.
relation_to_specdx: Uses LLM-generated program versions as an N-version oracle and treats behavioural disagreement as a failure signal, the same intuition as SpecDx's population of executors; SpecDx asks a different question (is the specification, not the program, defective?) and adds a statistical latent model plus logical refutation to separate executor error from specification defects.
baseline_notes: Adaptation: for each scenario step, ask each model to synthesise k reference implementations of the step from T only (Tell variants as prompts), execute them on the scenario's database state, and flag a cell when the majority reference outcome differs from the specification's declared value d_c (spec-vs-reference disagreement) or when references split (ambiguity). Inputs: T, the scenario state, the checks C for comparison. It detects hidden requirements/mis-keys (all references differ from d_c) and some ambiguity, but not contradictions or weak checks, and gives no localisation within T. Code: no official repository found in the paper metadata; would require reimplementation.

title: SAC3: Reliable Hallucination Detection in Black-Box Language Models via Semantic-aware Cross-check Consistency
authors: Jiaxin Zhang; Zhuohang Li; Kamalika Das; Bradley Malin; Sricharan Kumar
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2023
subtopics: cross-model consistency; hallucination detection; question perturbation
summary: Finds that self-consistency checks miss question-level and model-level hallucinations and proposes SAC3, which adds semantically equivalent question perturbations and cross-model response checks with a verifier LM to sampling-based consistency.
relation_to_specdx: Combines input-rephrasing consistency (like SpecDx's Tell variants) with cross-model consistency (like SpecDx's model families), the closest NLP analogue of B4; it scores answer reliability, whereas SpecDx contrasts consensus against an anchored specification value to type specification defects.
baseline_notes: Map question perturbations to Tell variants and the verifier/cross-check models to other families: per cell, SAC3 score = weighted inconsistency of readings across variants (self) and across families (cross). Flag cells with high cross-check inconsistency. Reimplementation needed (no verified official code found); entirely black-box and offline with local models.

title: SelfCheckGPT: Zero-Resource Black-Box Hallucination Detection for Generative Large Language Models
authors: Potsawee Manakul; Adian Liusie; Mark Gales
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
subtopics: sampling-based uncertainty; hallucination detection; black-box consistency
summary: Proposes SelfCheckGPT, a zero-resource black-box hallucination detector that samples several responses from the same LLM and scores each sentence of the main response by its consistency (BERTScore, QA, n-gram, NLI or prompting variants) with the samples; inconsistent facts are flagged as likely hallucinations.
relation_to_specdx: Shares the premise that disagreement among stochastic samples signals unreliability; SpecDx instead uses the cross-family pattern of agreement against an anchored specification value to separate specification defects (consistent deviation) from agent errors (scattered deviation), whereas SelfCheckGPT treats consistency only as evidence of model correctness.
baseline_notes: B4 analogue. For each cell c (table,row,column at a scenario step) treat the declared value d_c as the 'main response' and the readings of all runs (models x Tell variants x seeds) as the samples; SelfCheck-Ngram/NLI score = 1 - support of d_c among runs. High score => flag cell as defective. It cannot type the defect (contradiction/hidden requirement/ambiguity/weak check) and conflates 'everyone disagrees with the anchor' (spec defect) with 'runs disagree among themselves' (ambiguity or agent error). Code: pip package selfcheckgpt (MIT), runs offline with local HF models; the NLI/n-gram variants work on short categorical cell values after verbalising them.

title: Semantic Uncertainty: Linguistic Invariances for Uncertainty Estimation in Natural Language Generation
authors: Lorenz Kuhn; Yarin Gal; Sebastian Farquhar
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2023)
subtopics: sampling-based uncertainty; semantic entropy; semantic equivalence
summary: Introduces semantic entropy: sample several generations, cluster them into meaning-equivalence classes with bidirectional entailment, and compute entropy over the classes; it predicts QA accuracy better than token-level baselines without model modification.
relation_to_specdx: Semantic entropy over meaning clusters is the single-model analogue of SpecDx's B4 inter-family disagreement entropy; SpecDx goes further by anchoring readings to the specification's declared value, modelling executor accuracy and item difficulty, and separating ambiguity (two stable readings) from agent noise, which entropy alone conflates.
baseline_notes: B4 analogue. Per cell c, collect the readings of all runs (models x Tell variants x seeds) for that scenario step; cluster readings by exact value for categorical/numeric cells or by bidirectional NLI for free-text outcomes; compute entropy over clusters (pooled, or per family then averaged). High entropy => ambiguity flag. Offline with a local NLI model. It cannot detect hidden requirements where every run agrees on a value different from d_c (entropy is low), so pair it with anchor disagreement for a fair comparison.

title: We’re Afraid Language Models Aren’t Modeling Ambiguity
authors: Alisa Liu; Zhaofeng Wu; Julian Michael; Alane Suhr; Peter West; Alexander Koller; Swabha Swayamdipta; Noah Smith; Yejin Choi
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
subtopics: ambiguity; natural language inference; benchmark
summary: Characterises ambiguity in a sentence by its effect on entailment relations and releases AmbiEnt, a linguist-annotated benchmark of 1,645 NLI examples with diverse ambiguity types; tests show that pretrained LMs (including GPT-4) rarely recognise or disentangle the possible readings.
relation_to_specdx: Its entailment-based definition of ambiguity (a premise entails different hypotheses under different readings) is close to SpecDx's entailment set A_c; SpecDx operationalises this at the level of executable cells and detects it from executor behaviour rather than asking a model whether a sentence is ambiguous, and the paper's finding that single LMs miss ambiguity motivates a population-based detector.

title: JEST: N+1-Version Differential Testing of Both JavaScript Engines and Specification
authors: Jihyeok Park; Seungmin An; Dongjun Youn; Gyeongwon Kim; Sukyoung Ryu
venue: 2021 IEEE/ACM 43rd International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE)
subtopics: N+1-version differential testing; specification bugs; statistical localisation; ECMAScript
specdx_components: defect taxonomy; family effects/correlated errors; ddmin; baseline B2
summary: Proposes N+1-version differential testing: synthesise programs from the ECMAScript specification, inject assertions derived from the specification's semantics into conformance tests, run them on several JavaScript engines, treat a failure shared by most engines as a specification bug and a minority failure as an engine bug, and localise specification bugs statistically; JEST found 44 engine bugs and 27 bugs in ES11.
relation_to_specdx: The closest precedent for SpecDx's core move: the specification is one more fallible 'version', and a deviation shared by most independent implementations indicts the specification rather than the implementations, with statistical localisation in the spec text. SpecDx differs in using stochastic LLM interpreters of a business specification (so it needs an explicit reliability/difficulty model rather than majority voting over near-correct engines), in typing defects (contradiction, hidden requirement, ambiguity, weak check) with MUS/MCS refutation and witnesses, and in handling set-valued truth.
baseline_notes: JEST's decision rule is directly applicable to SpecDx's run matrix: for each cell, if the fraction of interpreters (or families) whose reading differs from d_c exceeds a threshold (JEST uses 'all but a minority'), label the cell a specification defect, else label deviating runs as agent errors; localisation in T can mimic JEST's spectrum-based ranking over sentences. This equals the 'anchor-only / majority vote' simulation baseline and is a principled named counterpart to it. The JEST code itself (Scala, ECMAScript-specific) cannot be reused; reimplement the rule (a few lines).

title: Coverage-directed differential testing of JVM implementations
authors: Yuting Chen; Ting Su; Chengnian Sun; Zhendong Su; Jianjun Zhao
venue: Proceedings of the 37th ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation
subtopics: differential testing; coverage-directed fuzzing; MCMC mutator selection; specification ambiguity
summary: Proposes classfuzz, which mutates seed classfiles with predefined mutators chosen by MCMC sampling, keeps mutants with unique coverage on a reference JVM, and runs them on several JVMs to expose discrepancies; it raises the discrepancy-triggering ratio from 1.7% to 11.9%, and several of the 62 reported discrepancies matched clarifications later made to the JVM specification.
relation_to_specdx: Shows that discrepancies among implementations can reveal gaps in the specification itself, and guides input generation adaptively, both ideas central to SpecDx; it relies on a human to decide whether a discrepancy is a JVM bug or a specification issue, which SpecDx automates through its latent model and refutation.

title: ClarifyCodeBench: Evaluating LLMs on Clarifying Ambiguous Requirements for Code Generation
authors: Zheng Fang; Dongming Jin; Yihong dong; Yongmin Li; Kechi Zhang; Zhi Jin; Ge Li
venue: arXiv
subtopics: clarifying questions; ambiguous requirements; code generation benchmark
summary: ClarifyCodeBench is an interactive benchmark that evaluates whether LLMs resolve ambiguous, incomplete or underspecified code-generation requirements by asking clarifying questions instead of coding one-shot.
relation_to_specdx: A 2026 benchmark of requirement defects in code generation; it evaluates a single model's clarification behaviour, whereas SpecDx detects such defects from population behaviour without interaction.

title: Do Code Language Models Follow Tests? Paired Interventions on Program Behavior
authors: Yunhao Liang; Chengguang Gan; Ruixuan Ying; Hanjun Wei; Zhe Cui; Shiwen Ni
venue: arXiv
subtopics: tests as specification; underspecification; test following
summary: Measures whether code LMs follow the rule expressed by visible tests by holding an underspecified description fixed and changing example outputs to express one of two valid rules; switching rates across five models range from 11.1% to 65.8%.
relation_to_specdx: Directly probes how executors weigh NL text versus executable examples when the text admits two readings, the situation SpecDx models with set-valued entailment sets anchored by d_c; it suggests executor accuracy toward anchors varies widely by model.

title: Galápagos: Automated N-Version Programming with LLMs
authors: Javier Ron; Diogo Gaspar; Javier Cabrera-Arteaga; Benoit Baudry; Martin Monperrus
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
subtopics: N-version programming; LLM-generated program variants; diversity
summary: Galápagos uses LLMs to generate diverse variants of real-world C functions, validates their correctness and equivalence, and assembles N-version binaries, showing that the variants are provably equivalent yet diverse enough to tolerate some faults.
relation_to_specdx: Revives N-version programming with LLMs as the source of diversity, the same population idea SpecDx uses; Galápagos targets runtime fault tolerance of programs, whereas SpecDx uses LLM 'versions' of a specification's interpretation to diagnose the specification.

title: Benchmarking Uncertainty Quantification Methods for Large Language Models with LM-Polygraph
authors: Roman Vashurin; Ekaterina Fadeeva; Artem Vazhentsev; Lyudmila Rvanova; Daniil Vasilev; Akim Tsvigun; Sergey Petrakov; Rui Xing; Abdelrahman Sadallah; Kirill Grishchenkov; Alexander Panchenko; Timothy Baldwin; Preslav Nakov; Maxim Panov; Artem Shelmanov
venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
subtopics: uncertainty quantification; benchmark
summary: Introduces a benchmark built on LM-Polygraph that implements state-of-the-art UQ baselines and evaluates them consistently across text generation tasks, including confidence normalisation, in a large empirical study.
relation_to_specdx: The most systematic comparison of the disagreement and uncertainty measures that SpecDx's B4 baseline family draws on; it helps choose which B4 variants to report.

title: Learning to Ask: When LLM Agents Meet Unclear Instruction
authors: Wenxuan Wang; Shi Juluan; Zixuan Ling; Yuk-Kit Chan; Chaozheng Wang; Cheryl Lee; Youliang Yuan; Jen-tse Huang; Wenxiang Jiao; Michael R. Lyu
venue: Proceedings of the 2025 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
subtopics: tool-use agents; unclear instructions; benchmark
summary: Analyses real user instructions to tool-using LLM agents, builds Noisy ToolBench with imperfect (e.g. missing-argument) instructions, finds agents tend to hallucinate missing arguments, and proposes a framework that prompts agents to ask questions when instructions are unclear.
relation_to_specdx: Shows that tool-using agents fill specification gaps by guessing, which is the behaviour that makes SpecDx's populations informative: guesses scatter across agents for underspecified inputs, producing ambiguity signatures.

title: Look Before You Leap: An Exploratory Study of Uncertainty Analysis for Large Language Models
authors: Yuheng Huang; Jiayang Song; Zhijie Wang; Shengming Zhao; Huaming Chen; Felix Juefei-Xu; Lei Ma
venue: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering
subtopics: uncertainty estimation; SE study; code generation
summary: An exploratory SE study applying twelve uncertainty estimation methods to LLMs across NLP and code generation tasks, assessing how well uncertainty signals reveal erroneous predictions.
relation_to_specdx: Shows that sampling- and model-based uncertainty only partially predicts LLM errors in SE tasks; SpecDx uses disagreement not to predict model errors but to diagnose specifications.

title: What Prompts Don't Say: Understanding and Managing Underspecification in LLM Prompts
authors: Chenyang Yang; Yike Shi; Qianou Ma; Michael Xieyang Liu; Christian Kästner; Tongshuang Wu
venue: arXiv
subtopics: prompt underspecification; requirements; LLM applications
summary: Analyses underspecified prompts: LLMs infer unspecified requirements 41.1% of the time, but such behaviour is fragile (twice as likely to regress across model or prompt changes), and specifying everything does not reliably help because requirements can conflict; requirements-aware prompt optimisation improves performance by 4.8%.
relation_to_specdx: Documents that unspecified requirements are filled inconsistently across models and prompts, which is the variation SpecDx exploits with model families and Tell variants to expose hidden requirements.

title: B4: Towards Optimal Assessment of Plausible Code Solutions with Plausible Tests
authors: Mouxiang Chen; Zhongxin Liu; He Tao; Yusu Hong; David Lo; Xin Xia; Jianling Sun
venue: Proceedings of the 39th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering
subtopics: code-test agreement; Bayesian selection; plausible tests
summary: Shows that, in a Bayesian framework, the optimal strategy for selecting among plausible generated code solutions using plausible generated tests is defined by the posterior of passing states, and derives an efficient approximation (B4) that outperforms heuristic code-test agreement strategies.
relation_to_specdx: A principled latent-variable treatment of mutually unreliable code and tests, close in spirit to SpecDx's treatment of the specification checks as a fallible rater; it aims to pick a correct program, not to diagnose the tests or the specification.

title: Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs
authors: Miao Xiong; Zhiyuan Hu; Xinyang Lu; Yifei Li; Jie Fu; Junxian He; Bryan Hooi
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2024)
subtopics: verbalised uncertainty; confidence elicitation; calibration
summary: Benchmarks black-box confidence elicitation along prompting (verbalised confidence), sampling and aggregation; LLMs verbalising confidence are overconfident, calibration improves with scale but stays far from ideal, and consistency among multiple samples helps mitigate overconfidence.
relation_to_specdx: Shows that self-reported confidence is unreliable and that sample consistency is a better signal, which supports SpecDx's choice of behavioural readings over asking interpreters whether T is ambiguous; it concerns per-answer confidence, not specification defects.
baseline_notes: A verbalised-confidence variant of B1 (ask each model how confident it is that d_c follows from T) could be added cheaply, but it is a prompt strategy rather than a distinct method.

title: CLAMBER: A Benchmark of Identifying and Clarifying Ambiguous Information Needs in Large Language Models
authors: Tong Zhang; Peixin Qin; Yang Deng; Chen Huang; Wenqiang Lei; Junhong Liu; Dingnan Jin; Hongru Liang; Tat-Seng Chua
venue: Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
subtopics: ambiguity; clarifying questions; benchmark; taxonomy
summary: Presents CLAMBER, a taxonomy-driven benchmark of about 12K queries for evaluating whether LLMs identify and clarify ambiguous information needs; off-the-shelf LLMs show limited ability, and CoT or few-shot prompting can make them overconfident.
relation_to_specdx: Provides a taxonomy of ambiguity (epistemic misalignment, ambiguity, aleatoric output) and evidence that single LLMs are poor ambiguity judges, supporting SpecDx's choice of a behavioural population oracle over self-reported ambiguity; it targets user queries, not executable specifications.

title: DiffSpec: Differential Testing with LLMs using Natural Language Specifications and Code Artifacts
authors: Nikitha Rao; Elizabeth Gilbert; Harrison Green; Tahina Ramananandro; Nikhil Swamy; Claire Le Goues; Sarah Fakhoury
venue: arXiv
subtopics: LLM-based differential testing; natural-language specifications; test generation
summary: DiffSpec uses prompt chaining over natural-language specifications (e.g. ISA documents, RFCs), bug reports and code to make LLMs generate targeted differential tests; it produced 1,901 differentiating tests for eBPF runtimes and 299 for Wasm validators, revealing confirmed bugs.
relation_to_specdx: LLMs read a natural-language specification to synthesise inputs that split implementations, close to SpecDx's clause-guided scenario synthesis; DiffSpec blames implementations, whereas SpecDx's executors are LLMs and the target is the specification.

title: Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
authors: Yilun Du; Shuang Li; Antonio Torralba; Joshua B. Tenenbaum; Igor Mordatch
venue: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024)
subtopics: multi-agent debate; cross-model agreement
summary: Has several LLM instances propose answers and debate them over multiple rounds until they converge on a common answer, improving mathematical and strategic reasoning and reducing hallucinated facts.
relation_to_specdx: Debate deliberately makes agents' answers dependent, which is the opposite of SpecDx's requirement of independent readings across families; SpecDx keeps interpreters isolated so that agreement is evidence about the specification rather than a product of persuasion.

title: Kernel Language Entropy: Fine-grained Uncertainty Quantification for LLMs from Semantic Similarities
authors: Alexander Nikitin; Jannik Kossen; Yarin Gal; Pekka Marttinen
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37
subtopics: semantic uncertainty; kernel entropy; sampling-based uncertainty
summary: Kernel Language Entropy generalises semantic entropy by computing the von Neumann entropy of a positive semidefinite kernel over pairwise semantic similarities of sampled answers, capturing graded rather than all-or-nothing equivalence.
relation_to_specdx: A finer-grained version of the entropy statistic behind B4, useful where readings are partially similar (e.g. near-equal numeric values or overlapping text); like semantic entropy it lacks an anchor and executor model.
baseline_notes: Variant of the semantic-entropy B4 with a similarity kernel over cell readings (e.g. numeric distance or NLI). Official code (BSD-3-Clause-Clear) builds on the semantic_uncertainty codebase; runs offline.

title: CodeT: Code Generation with Generated Tests
authors: Bei Chen; Fengji Zhang; Anh Nguyen; Daoguang Zan; Zeqi Lin; Jian-Guang Lou; Weizhu Chen
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2023)
subtopics: dual execution agreement; generated tests; code generation
summary: CodeT has the same LLM generate both code samples and test cases, then ranks samples by dual execution agreement, i.e. consistency of a solution's outputs with generated tests and with other solutions; it improves HumanEval pass@1 to 65.8%.
relation_to_specdx: Jointly scores two fallible artefacts (code and tests) by their mutual agreement, analogous to SpecDx scoring interpreters and the specification's checks against each other; CodeT selects code, while SpecDx targets defects in the checks and requirements.

title: LM-Polygraph: Uncertainty Estimation for Language Models
authors: Ekaterina Fadeeva; Roman Vashurin; Akim Tsvigun; Artem Vazhentsev; Sergey Petrakov; Kirill Fedyanin; Daniil Vasilev; Elizaveta Goncharova; Alexander Panchenko; Maxim Panov; Timothy Baldwin; Artem Shelmanov
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing: System Demonstrations
subtopics: uncertainty estimation toolkit; software
summary: LM-Polygraph is a Python framework implementing a battery of uncertainty estimation methods for LLM text generation behind unified interfaces, with a benchmark and a demo application.
relation_to_specdx: A ready, offline toolkit for computing many black-box disagreement-based uncertainty scores (lexical similarity, NumSemSets, EigV, semantic entropy) that can serve as B4 variants on SpecDx's run populations.
baseline_notes: Provides implementations of black-box sampling-based estimators that accept lists of sampled strings; feed each cell's readings across runs to obtain a battery of B4-style scores in one place (MIT).

title: LM vs LM: Detecting Factual Errors via Cross Examination
authors: Roi Cohen; May Hamri; Mor Geva; Amir Globerson
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
subtopics: cross-examination; inconsistency detection; multi-LM interaction
summary: Detects factual errors by cross-examination: an examiner LM questions the LM that made a claim over multiple turns to surface inconsistencies, outperforming existing factuality methods on four benchmarks.
relation_to_specdx: Inconsistency elicited by a second model as evidence of error resembles SpecDx's directed LLM probes for refutation; SpecDx targets specification claims and requires witness states rather than conversational inconsistency.

title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
authors: Xuezhi Wang; Jason Wei; Dale Schuurmans; Quoc V. Le; Ed H. Chi; Sharan Narang; Aakanksha Chowdhery; Denny Zhou
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2023)
subtopics: sampling-based uncertainty; self-consistency; majority vote
summary: Replaces greedy chain-of-thought decoding with self-consistency: sample many reasoning paths and return the most frequent final answer, marginalising over paths; this gives large accuracy gains on arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks (e.g. GSM8K +17.9%).
relation_to_specdx: Self-consistency (majority vote over samples) is the aggregation inside SpecDx's B1 static-review baseline and the majority-vote baseline of its simulation study; it assumes one correct answer per input, whereas SpecDx models set-valued truth and treats systematic agreement against the anchor as evidence of a specification defect rather than of the answer.
baseline_notes: Used as the aggregation inside B1 and the simulation's majority-vote baseline rather than as a standalone baseline.

title: HDiff: A Semi-automatic Framework for Discovering Semantic Gap Attack in HTTP Implementations
authors: Kaiwen Shen; Jianyu Lu; Yaru Yang; Jianjun Chen; Mingming Zhang; Haixin Duan; Jia Zhang; Xiaofeng Zheng
venue: 2022 52nd Annual IEEE/IFIP International Conference on Dependable Systems and Networks (DSN)
subtopics: differential testing; specification rule extraction; semantic gap; HTTP
summary: HDiff extracts rules from HTTP specifications with NLP and uses differential testing across HTTP implementations to discover semantic gap attacks, i.e. inconsistent interpretations of the same request along a processing chain.
relation_to_specdx: Combines specification text mining with differential execution to find divergent interpretations of one specification; SpecDx applies the idea to LLM interpreters and attributes divergence to specification ambiguity versus executor error.

title: Natural Language to Code Translation with Execution
authors: Freda Shi; Daniel Fried; Marjan Ghazvininejad; Luke Zettlemoyer; Sida I. Wang
venue: Proceedings of the 2022 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
subtopics: execution agreement; minimum Bayes risk; code generation
summary: Introduces MBR-EXEC, which samples candidate programs, executes them on test inputs, and selects the program whose execution results agree most with the others, marginalising over semantically equivalent implementations.
relation_to_specdx: Execution-result clustering of sampled programs is the mechanism later reused by ClarifyGPT for ambiguity detection and is analogous to SpecDx clustering runs by cell values; MBR-EXEC picks the consensus, whereas SpecDx asks whether the consensus contradicts the specification.

title: AmbigQA: Answering Ambiguous Open-domain Questions
authors: Sewon Min; Julian Michael; Hannaneh Hajishirzi; Luke Zettlemoyer
venue: Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
subtopics: ambiguity; question answering; multiple answers
summary: Introduces AmbigQA, an open-domain QA task in which a system must find every plausible answer to a question and rewrite the question once per answer, together with the AmbigNQ dataset (14,042 NQ-open questions); over half of NQ-open questions turn out to be ambiguous.
relation_to_specdx: Establishes that a natural-language input can admit a set of valid answers, which matches SpecDx's set-valued entailment set A_c = {x,y} for an ambiguous cell; AmbigQA relies on human annotation of the answer set, whereas SpecDx infers it automatically from a population of executors.

title: RFC-directed differential testing of certificate validation in SSL/TLS implementations
authors: Chu Chen; Cong Tian; Zhenhua Duan; Liang Zhao
venue: Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Software Engineering
subtopics: differential testing; RFC-directed test generation; specification rules; symbolic execution
summary: Generates test certificates directed by rules extracted from RFC 5280 (expressed as a symbolic program and explored by dynamic symbolic execution) and uses them for differential testing of certificate validation across SSL/TLS implementations, targeting conformance to the RFC rather than random mutation.
relation_to_specdx: Derives test inputs from the clauses of a natural-language standard and solves for inputs that exercise each rule, similar to SpecDx taking boundary values from the clauses and using symbolic search for witness states; the RFC is assumed correct, whereas SpecDx questions the specification.

title: NEZHA: Efficient Domain-Independent Differential Testing
authors: Theofilos Petsios; Adrian Tang; Salvatore Stolfo; Angelos D. Keromytis; Suman Jana
venue: 2017 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (SP)
subtopics: differential testing; delta-diversity; guided input generation
summary: Presents NEZHA, a domain-independent differential testing framework that guides input generation (gray-box and black-box) by delta-diversity, a metric of behavioural asymmetries among the programs under test; it finds differences 52 and 27 times faster than Frankencerts and Mucerts on certificate validation.
relation_to_specdx: Delta-diversity, i.e. steering inputs toward those that split implementations, is a heuristic form of SpecDx's information-gain scenario selection; SpecDx selects scenarios to discriminate between specification-defect and agent-error hypotheses under a probabilistic model rather than to maximise raw discrepancy.
baseline_notes: Repository confirmed via its README (cites the S&P 2017 paper); GitHub API metadata unavailable (rate limit).

title: Using Frankencerts for Automated Adversarial Testing of Certificate Validation in SSL/TLS Implementations
authors: Chad Brubaker; Suman Jana; Baishakhi Ray; Sarfraz Khurshid; Vitaly Shmatikov
venue: 2014 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
subtopics: differential testing; certificate validation; mutation-based input generation
summary: Introduces frankencerts, synthetic X.509 certificates assembled from mutated parts of real certificates, and uses differential testing across SSL/TLS libraries (a discrepancy between accepting and rejecting implementations is the oracle); it uncovered 208 discrepancies, many of them serious vulnerabilities.
relation_to_specdx: Uses disagreement among independent implementations of one specification as an oracle and synthesises boundary inputs to provoke it, as SpecDx's active scenario synthesis does; frankencerts attributes discrepancies to implementation flaws, while SpecDx explicitly models the alternative that the specification itself is defective.

title: Finding and understanding bugs in C compilers
authors: Xuejun Yang; Yang Chen; Eric Eide; John Regehr
venue: Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGPLAN Conference on Programming Language Design and Implementation
subtopics: differential testing; random program generation; compiler testing
summary: Presents Csmith, a randomised generator of valid C programs free of undefined behaviour, used for three years of differential testing of C compilers; it found more than 325 previously unknown bugs, and every compiler tested both crashed and silently miscompiled valid input.
relation_to_specdx: The canonical case of using several implementations as cross-referencing oracles with majority voting on outputs; SpecDx inherits the voting idea but applies it to LLM interpreters of a natural-language specification and adds a latent model of interpreter reliability, since its 'implementations' are far less reliable than compilers.

title: Modeling software design diversity: a review
authors: Bev Littlewood; Peter Popov; Lorenzo Strigini
venue: ACM Computing Surveys
subtopics: design diversity; failure dependence; survey
summary: Tutorial survey of probabilistic models of software design diversity, explaining why the independence of version failures is untenable and how dependence must be assessed to evaluate the reliability of diverse fault-tolerant systems.
relation_to_specdx: A reference survey for the correlated-error assumption underlying SpecDx's identifiability theory and for how dependence between versions (here, model families) can be modelled.

title: Differential Testing for Software
authors: William M. McKeeman
venue: Digital Technical Journal, 10(1)
subtopics: differential testing; foundational
summary: Introduces differential testing as a technique: run the same test input through several comparable implementations (C compilers at DEC) and treat any disagreement as a candidate bug to be investigated.
relation_to_specdx: The origin of the cross-implementation oracle that SpecDx generalises to LLM interpreters of a business specification; McKeeman assumes a correct specification and blames implementations.

title: Analysis of faults in an N-version software experiment
authors: S.S. Brilliant; J.C. Knight; N.G. Leveson
venue: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering
subtopics: N-version programming; fault analysis; specification-induced faults
summary: Analyses the faults found in the 27 versions of the Knight-Leveson N-version experiment, examining which faults caused coincident failures across versions.
relation_to_specdx: Fault-level evidence about why independently developed versions of one specification fail together; relevant to whether SpecDx's consensus deviations come from the specification or from shared difficulty.

title: The N-Version Approach to Fault-Tolerant Software
authors: A. Avizienis
venue: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering
subtopics: N-version programming; design diversity
summary: Defines N-version programming as the independent generation of N>=2 functionally equivalent programs from the same initial specification, executed in parallel with a decision algorithm that takes a consensus or majority output.
relation_to_specdx: SpecDx's population of LLM interpreters is an N-version system in which every 'version' is generated from the same specification T; SpecDx inverts the use of the vote, treating a consensus that contradicts the specification's checks as evidence of a specification defect.

title: Coding Agents Are Guessing: Measuring Action-Boundary Violations in Underspecified DevOps Instructions
authors: Zimo Ji; Zekai Zhang; Congying Xu; Zongjie Li; Yudong Gao; Shuai Wang; Shing-Chi Cheung
venue: arXiv
subtopics: underspecified instructions; coding agents; benchmark
summary: UnderSpecBench measures action-boundary violations by coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) on DevOps tasks with benign but underspecified instructions, across 69 task families grounded in documented incidents.
relation_to_specdx: Shows that agents guess under underspecification in operational settings; SpecDx turns such guessing, observed across a population, into evidence about where the specification is underspecified.

title: Hallucinating Certificates: Differential Testing of TLS Certificate Validation Using Generative Language Models
authors: Muhammad Talha Paracha; Kyle Posluns; Kevin Borgolte; Martina Lindorfer; David Choffnes
venue: Proceedings of the 2026 IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering
subtopics: LLM-based differential testing; certificate validation; generative input synthesis
summary: Introduces MLCerts, which uses generative language models to synthesise X.509 certificates for differential testing of TLS certificate validation across libraries, exploiting models' tendency to produce syntactically valid but semantically unusual inputs.
relation_to_specdx: A recent example of LLMs used as input generators for differential testing; SpecDx instead uses LLMs as the implementations (interpreters) being compared, with the specification as an anchored, possibly defective, rater.

title: Uncertainty Decomposition for Clarification Seeking in LLM Agents
authors: Gregory Matsnev
venue: arXiv
subtopics: uncertainty decomposition; clarification seeking; agents
summary: Proposes a prompt-based method that decomposes an LLM agent's uncertainty (including underspecification) to decide when to seek clarification, under black-box and latency constraints that rule out multi-sampling.
relation_to_specdx: Agent-side, single-run self-assessment of underspecification; SpecDx relies on multi-run, multi-family behaviour rather than self-reported uncertainty.

title: Mokav: Execution-driven differential testing with LLMs
authors: Khashayar Etemadi; Bardia Mohammadi; Zhendong Su; Martin Monperrus
venue: Journal of Systems and Software
subtopics: LLM-based differential testing; difference-exposing tests
summary: Mokav iteratively prompts an LLM with execution feedback to generate a difference-exposing test, an input on which two program versions produce provably different outputs.
relation_to_specdx: An LLM-driven search for discriminating inputs, comparable to SpecDx's directed LLM probe for witness states; SpecDx's witnesses refute specification-defect candidates rather than distinguish two programs.

title: Aligning Language Models to Explicitly Handle Ambiguity
authors: Hyuhng Joon Kim; Youna Kim; Cheonbok Park; Junyeob Kim; Choonghyun Park; Kang Min Yoo; Sang-goo Lee; Taeuk Kim
venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
subtopics: ambiguity; alignment; perceived ambiguity
summary: Proposes Alignment with Perceived Ambiguity (APA), which trains LLMs to recognise and handle ambiguous queries using the model's own perceived ambiguity (measured through its knowledge) as the training signal.
relation_to_specdx: Treats ambiguity as model-relative, in line with SpecDx's view that ambiguity is defined by the readings of competent interpreters; it changes model behaviour rather than diagnosing the input text.

title: Tell Me More! Towards Implicit User Intention Understanding of Language Model Driven Agents
authors: Cheng Qian; Bingxiang He; Zhong Zhuang; Jia Deng; Yujia Qin; Xin Cong; Zhong Zhang; Jie Zhou; Yankai Lin; Zhiyuan Liu; Maosong Sun
venue: Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
subtopics: agents; vague instructions; clarification; benchmark
summary: Introduces the Intention-in-Interaction (IN3) benchmark for implicit user intentions in agent tasks and trains Mistral-Interact to assess task vagueness, ask about missing details and refine them into actionable goals before execution.
relation_to_specdx: Agent-side handling of vague task specifications; SpecDx instead diagnoses the specification offline from many agents' behaviour.

title: A Matter of TASTE: Improving Coverage and Difficulty of Agent Benchmarks
authors: Tomer Keren; Nitay Calderon; Asaf Yehudai; Yotam Perlitz; Michal Shmueli-Scheuer; Roi Reichart
venue: arXiv
subtopics: automatic task synthesis; tau2-bench; tool-sequence coverage; difficulty evolution
summary: TASTE reverses benchmark task construction: an adaptive contrastive n-gram model trained on LLM-judged validity samples valid tool sequences, representative sequences are chosen by clustering, instantiated into tasks and made harder by iterative difficulty evolution, giving tau^c-Bench, an extension of tau2-Bench's three domains (built on the tau-Bench-Verified task sets) on which near-saturated agents drop sharply and tool-combination coverage more than doubles.
relation_to_specdx: Automatic scenario synthesis in exactly SpecDx's benchmark family (tau2-Bench airline/retail/telecom). TASTE aims at coverage and difficulty for agent evaluation and relies on LLM validity judges; SpecDx aims at information about specification defects and could reuse TASTE's coverage-oriented generator as a scenario pool.

title: Fluid Language Model Benchmarking
authors: Valentin Hofmann; David Heineman; Ian Magnusson; Kyle Lo; Jesse Dodge; Maarten Sap; Pang Wei Koh; Chun Wang; Hannaneh Hajishirzi; Noah A. Smith
venue: Second Conference on Language Modeling (COLM 2025)
subtopics: computerized adaptive testing; IRT; LLM benchmarking; dynamic item selection
summary: Fluid Benchmarking fits an item response model on existing LM evaluation results and selects items dynamically per model, as in computerised adaptive testing; it beats random sampling and other IRT baselines in efficiency, validity, variance and saturation (e.g., higher validity and lower variance on MMLU with fifty times fewer items).
relation_to_specdx: The most recent LLM-side CAT method and a natural adaptive-selection baseline: it chooses items to estimate model ability, whereas SpecDx chooses scenarios to estimate item (specification-cell) defect status. Its released IRT tooling could be repurposed with roles swapped.
baseline_notes: CAT selection baseline: fit a 2PL IRT on the interpreter x scenario-cell deviation matrix (as B3), then pick the next scenario cell by maximum Fisher information at the current item-parameter uncertainty (roles swapped: estimate cell parameters, query interpreters). Inputs: the reading matrix. Code: allenai/fluid-benchmarking on GitHub (linked from the official HF dataset card; stars/licence not checked because the GitHub API was rate-limited).
verified_by: proceedings page https://openreview.net/forum?id=mxcCg9YRqj (OpenReview API record, venue COLM 2025)

title: Position: AI Evaluation Should Learn from How We Test Humans
authors: Yan Zhuang; Qi Liu; Zachary Pardos; Patrick C. Kyllonen; Jiyun Zu; Zhenya Huang; Shijin Wang; Enhong Chen
venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 267 (position track)
subtopics: computerized adaptive testing; LLM evaluation; psychometrics; item quality
summary: Position paper (arXiv 2306.10512, earlier titled 'Efficiently Measuring the Cognitive Ability of LLMs: An Adaptive Testing Perspective') arguing that AI evaluation should move from static benchmarks to psychometric adaptive testing: estimate each item's characteristics and tailor the item sequence to each model, which also exposes low-quality or erroneous items.
relation_to_specdx: Shares the CAT view (item parameters plus adaptive selection) and the concern with erroneous benchmark items. SpecDx inverts the target: it measures the items (specification cells) using a population of models, and synthesises new scenarios rather than selecting from a fixed bank.

title: Reliable and Efficient Amortized Model-based Evaluation
authors: Sang T. Truong; Yuheng Tu; Percy Liang; Bo Li; Sanmi Koyejo
venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 267
subtopics: IRT; adaptive testing; amortized calibration; question generation
summary: Uses IRT to separate LM ability from question difficulty, trains a model that predicts difficulty from question content (amortised calibration), and trains a difficulty-conditioned question generator so that adaptive testing can generate informative questions on demand; across 22 benchmarks and 172 LMs this is more reliable and efficient than random subsets.
relation_to_specdx: Closest LLM-evaluation analogue of SpecDx's active scenario synthesis: adaptive selection plus generation of new test items guided by an item model. SpecDx generates business scenarios from clause literals and boundary values to diagnose the specification, not to rank models.

title: Trust or Escalate: LLM Judges with Provable Guarantees for Human Agreement
authors: Jaehun Jung; Faeze Brahman; Yejin Choi
venue: The Thirteenth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2025)
subtopics: cascaded evaluation; escalation; selective prediction; LLM judges
summary: Selective evaluation for LLM judges: estimate judge confidence (Simulated Annotators) and trust a judgment only when confident, giving a provable guarantee of human agreement; Cascaded Selective Evaluation starts with cheap judges and escalates to stronger models only when necessary while keeping the guarantee.
relation_to_specdx: Direct precedent for SpecDx's sequential escalation (cheap pilot, then the full committee) with a calibrated stopping rule. SpecDx escalates from one model per family to the whole population and its guarantee target is defect diagnosis, without human labels.

title: Modern Bayesian Experimental Design
authors: Tom Rainforth; Adam Foster; Desi R. Ivanova; Freddie Bickford Smith
venue: Statistical Science
subtopics: Bayesian experimental design; review; EIG estimation; adaptive design
summary: Review of modern Bayesian experimental design: how recent advances in EIG estimation, optimisation and amortised/adaptive policies overcome its computational challenges, and open directions.
relation_to_specdx: Up-to-date reference for EIG-based sequential design; SpecDx's scenario synthesis is a myopic adaptive BED over a discrete design space (scenario cells, boundary literals). Use to position the realised-information-gain reward against proper EIG estimators.

title: Active Surrogate Estimators: An Active Learning Approach to Label-Efficient Model Evaluation
authors: Jannik Kossen; Sebastian Farquhar; Yarin Gal; Thomas Rainforth
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35
subtopics: active testing; surrogate estimation; label-efficient evaluation; XWED
summary: Proposes Active Surrogate Estimators, which estimate model performance by interpolating the errors of unlabeled points with an actively learned surrogate instead of a Monte Carlo estimator, with an acquisition strategy (XWED) tailored to the final estimation task; more label-efficient than active testing on deep-network evaluation.
relation_to_specdx: SpecDx's cell model already acts as a surrogate that predicts the reading pattern of unrun scenario cells; ASE's XWED acquisition is a principled alternative to Thompson-EIG when the target is an aggregate (e.g., defect count). SpecDx's target is per-cell typed diagnosis.
baseline_notes: Use the SpecDx cell model as the surrogate; XWED acquisition picks the cell whose label most reduces expected error of the target estimate (e.g., number of defective cells). Code: jlko/active-surrogate-estimators (no licence file, notebooks; would need re-implementation of XWED).

title: Active Testing: Sample-Efficient Model Evaluation
authors: Jannik Kossen; Sebastian Farquhar; Yarin Gal; Tom Rainforth
venue: Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 139
subtopics: active testing; label-efficient evaluation; importance sampling; acquisition functions
summary: Defines active testing: choosing which test points to label so that model evaluation is sample-efficient, with acquisition strategies tailored to risk estimation (not training) and an unbiased importance-weighted estimator (LURE-style) that also reduces variance.
relation_to_specdx: Closest ML analogue of SpecDx's scenario selection: both spend a label/run budget to estimate a quantity rather than to train. SpecDx's 'label' is an execution by a committee of LLM interpreters and the target is a defect diagnosis per cell, not a risk estimate; active testing's bias-correction matters if SpecDx reports defect prevalence.
baseline_notes: Adapt: pool = candidate scenario cells; surrogate = current SpecDx cell model (or a cheap pilot model) giving predicted deviation probability per cell; acquisition q(cell) proportional to expected loss (here, predicted posterior entropy of defect label or predicted deviation); sample cells from q and run the committee; use LURE weights when estimating defect rate. Code: jlko/active-testing (MIT, Python, offline; acquisition code is generic over arrays).

title: Model-based exploration of the frontier of behaviours for deep learning system testing
authors: Vincenzo Riccio; Paolo Tonella
venue: Proceedings of the 28th ACM Joint Meeting on European Software Engineering Conference and Symposium on the Foundations of Software Engineering
subtopics: frontier of behaviours; boundary search; search-based testing; DL system testing
summary: Introduces the frontier of behaviours, the inputs at which a DL system starts to misbehave, and DeepJanus, a model-based search tool that generates pairs of similar inputs straddling that frontier; if the frontier lies inside the validity domain, the inputs reveal quality deficiencies (shown on lane keeping and MNIST).
relation_to_specdx: The SE counterpart of SpecDx's boundary values: both target the transition point where behaviour flips. DeepJanus searches a continuous model-based input space for one system; SpecDx takes boundary literals directly from executable clauses and asks whether a population of interpreters flips at the same place the specification does.
baseline_notes: Frontier-search baseline for scenario synthesis: represent a scenario by the clause-relevant parameters (amounts, dates, tiers), run a DeepJanus-style multi-objective search (pairs of nearby scenarios, one where the committee agrees with C and one where it does not; maximise sparseness, minimise pair distance) and feed the frontier scenarios to SpecDx's diagnosis.
