summary: Introduces WorkArena, 33 tasks on the ServiceNow enterprise platform that knowledge workers routinely perform, together with the BrowserGym environment for web agents, and reports a large gap between open and closed LLMs.
relation_to_specdx: An enterprise-workflow benchmark whose task validators are hand-written checks (C) over a real business platform; it assumes them correct, whereas SpecDx would audit such validators against the task text.

title: WorkArena++: Towards Compositional Planning and Reasoning-based Common Knowledge Work Tasks
authors: Léo Boisvert; Megh Thakkar; Maxime Gasse; Massimo Caccia; Thibault Le Sellier De Chezelles; Quentin Cappart; Nicolas Chapados; Alexandre Lacoste; Alexandre Drouin
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (NeurIPS 2024), Datasets and Benchmarks Track
subtopics: agent benchmark; enterprise workflows; compositional tasks
summary: WorkArena++ adds 682 compositional ServiceNow workflow tasks that test planning, arithmetic reasoning, retrieval and contextual understanding of web agents, compares LLMs/VLMs with human workers, and can generate ground-truth traces automatically.
relation_to_specdx: Compositional enterprise tasks with programmatic validators, a realistic setting where SpecDx-style auditing of validators against task descriptions could be applied; the paper does not question its validators.

title: WorkBench: a Benchmark Dataset for Agents in a Realistic Workplace Setting
authors: Olly Styles; Sam Miller; Patricia Cerda-Mardini; Tanaya Guha; Victor Sanchez; Bertie Vidgen
venue: Conference on Language Modeling (COLM 2024)
subtopics: agent benchmark; outcome-centric evaluation; golden end state
summary: WorkBench is a sandbox with five business databases, 26 tools and 690 workplace tasks whose success is judged by comparing the resulting database state with a unique ground-truth outcome (outcome-centric evaluation).
relation_to_specdx: Outcome-centric evaluation is the 'golden end state' clause type in SpecDx's C. WorkBench asserts each outcome is unique and unambiguous; SpecDx's ambiguity type tests exactly that assertion.
verified_by: proceedings page https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/329746 (COLM 2024, OpenReview forum 4HNAwZFDcH); arXiv 2405.00823

title: AI-augmented Business Process Management Systems: A Research Manifesto
authors: Marlon Dumas; Fabiana Fournier; Lior Limonad; Andrea Marrella; Marco Montali; Jana-Rebecca Rehse; Rafael Accorsi; Diego Calvanese; Giuseppe De Giacomo; Dirk Fahland; Avigdor Gal; Marcello La Rosa; Hagen Völzer; Ingo Weber
venue: ACM Transactions on Management Information Systems
subtopics: AI-augmented BPMS; manifesto
summary: Manifesto defining AI-augmented BPM systems (ABPMSs), process-aware information systems empowered by trustworthy AI that make process execution adaptable, proactive, explainable and context-sensitive, with their lifecycle, characteristics and research challenges.
relation_to_specdx: Frames the BPM community's agenda for AI-executed processes; SpecDx contributes a concrete technique for one challenge, validating the specification such systems execute.

title: Action-Based Conversations Dataset: A Corpus for Building More In-Depth Task-Oriented Dialogue Systems
authors: Derek Chen; Howard Chen; Yi Yang; Alexander Lin; Zhou Yu
venue: Proceedings of the 2021 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies
subtopics: task-oriented dialogue; agent guidelines; policy adherence
summary: ABCD is a corpus of over 10K human-to-human customer-service dialogues with 55 intents, each requiring a sequence of actions constrained by explicitly defined company policies; it introduces Action State Tracking and Cascading Dialogue Success tasks.
relation_to_specdx: An early dataset that operationalises business-policy adherence for agents, a predecessor of τ-bench's policy documents; it does not analyse defects in the guidelines.

title: Monotone Precision and Recall Measures for Comparing Executions and Specifications of Dynamic Systems
authors: Artem Polyvyanyy; Andreas Solti; Matthias Weidlich; Claudio Di Ciccio; Jan Mendling
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
subtopics: precision and recall; behavioural comparison; specification mining
summary: Introduces a framework of monotone precision and recall measures, based on topological entropy, for comparing a collection of execution traces with a specification of a dynamic system, including infinite behaviour.
relation_to_specdx: Precision (spec allows unseen behaviour) and recall (traces not allowed) are the quantitative counterparts of SpecDx's weak-check and hidden-requirement types; SpecDx computes cell-level, typed versions using executor populations.

title: Formal Modeling and SMT-Based Parameterized Verification of Data-Aware BPMN
authors: Diego Calvanese; Silvio Ghilardi; Alessandro Gianola; Marco Montali; Andrey Rivkin
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
subtopics: data-aware BPMN; SMT verification; artifact systems
summary: Proposes DAB, a data-aware BPMN extension operating over a read-only catalog and a read-write repository database, and verifies safety properties parametrically (for any catalog content and unboundedly many tuples) with array-based SMT techniques.
relation_to_specdx: Symbolic verification of processes over relational data is the closest formal counterpart to SpecDx's PostgreSQL-guarded procurement case; it checks a trusted model against properties rather than diagnosing the specification against its NL text.

title: Semantic DMN: Formalizing and Reasoning About Decisions in the Presence of Background Knowledge
authors: DIEGO CALVANESE; MARCO MONTALI; MARLON DUMAS; FABRIZIO M. MAGGI
venue: Theory and Practice of Logic Programming
subtopics: DMN; background knowledge; description logics
summary: Semantic DMN extends DMN decision models with background domain knowledge expressed in description logics, forming decision knowledge bases, and studies reasoning tasks such as consistency and completeness of decisions under that knowledge.
relation_to_specdx: Shows that table-level checks change once domain constraints are added, as SpecDx's clause analysis must account for database invariants; still purely symbolic.

title: Are we done with business process compliance: state of the art and challenges ahead
authors: Mustafa Hashmi; Guido Governatori; Ho-Pun Lam; Moe Thandar Wynn
venue: Knowledge and Information Systems
subtopics: business process compliance; survey
summary: Surveys 79 business process compliance papers (2000-2015), classifying approaches as design-time, run-time, auditing, framework-based or hybrid, and identifies open challenges.
relation_to_specdx: Compliance research assumes the normative rules are correct and checks processes against them; SpecDx targets defects in the rules themselves, a gap the survey's taxonomy does not cover.

title: Complete and Interpretable Conformance Checking of Business Processes
authors: Luciano Garcia-Banuelos; Nick R.T.P. van Beest; Marlon Dumas; Marcello La Rosa; Willem Mertens
venue: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering
subtopics: conformance checking; event structures; natural-language diagnostics
summary: Checks conformance by converting both the event log and the process model into event structures and aligning them with an error-correcting synchronized product, returning natural-language statements of behaviour allowed by the model but not observed and vice versa.
relation_to_specdx: Gives complete, interpretable two-sided diagnostics (model-only and log-only behaviour), analogous to SpecDx's distinction between weak checks and hidden requirements; it does not attribute deviations to model versus log errors.

title: Disambiguation of DMN Decision Tables
authors: Kimon Batoulis; Mathias Weske
venue: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
subtopics: DMN; ambiguity; overlapping rules
summary: Argues that DMN tables with overlapping rules are ambiguous and hard to analyse, and gives an algorithm that transforms them into equivalent tables with only exclusive rules, evaluated on synthetic tables.
relation_to_specdx: Treats rule overlap as ambiguity and resolves it syntactically; SpecDx detects ambiguity in the NL text from divergent executor readings and keeps it as a typed defect.

title: Aligning Textual and Graphical Descriptions of Processes Through ILP Techniques
authors: Josep Sànchez-Ferreres; Josep Carmona; Lluís Padró
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
subtopics: text-model alignment; ILP; NLP
summary: Aligns a textual process description with a graphical process model by extracting linguistic features of both and solving an integer linear program that yields an optimal alignment, outperforming the earlier technique.
relation_to_specdx: Optimal alignment of text sentences to model elements is a prerequisite for localising T-C mismatches; SpecDx localises in T by ddmin with an executor oracle instead of a linguistic alignment.

title: Anti-alignments in Conformance Checking – The Dark Side of Process Models
authors: Thomas Chatain; Josep Carmona
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
subtopics: anti-alignments; precision; witness runs
summary: Introduces anti-alignments, model runs that differ as much as possible from all observed traces, to estimate the precision of a process model without exploring its full state space.
relation_to_specdx: An anti-alignment is a witness that the model admits behaviour far from observations, analogous to SpecDx's witness states that refute or confirm a weak check.

title: Process Mining: Data Science in Action
authors: Wil van der Aalst
subtopics: process mining; conformance checking; textbook
summary: Wil van der Aalst's textbook (2nd ed., 2016) on process mining: discovering process models from event logs, checking conformance of models against logs, and enhancing models with data.
relation_to_specdx: Foundation for treating agent runs as an event log checked against a specification; SpecDx's twist is that deviations shared across many executors indict the specification rather than the executors.

title: Detecting Inconsistencies Between Process Models and Textual Descriptions
authors: Han van der Aa; Henrik Leopold; Hajo A. Reijers
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
subtopics: text-model inconsistency; NLP
summary: First approach to automatically identify inconsistencies between a process model and a corresponding textual description, detecting different activity orders and model activities missing from the text; evaluated on 46 real-life model-text pairs.
relation_to_specdx: BPM 2015 predecessor of van der Aa et al. (IS 2017); same relation to SpecDx.

title: On the Discovery of Declarative Control Flows for Artful Processes
authors: Claudio Di Ciccio; Massimo Mecella
venue: ACM Transactions on Management Information Systems
subtopics: Declare discovery; MINERful; statistical support
summary: MINERful discovers declarative control-flow constraints from logs in two phases: it builds a knowledge base of statistics extracted from the log and then queries it to infer Declare constraints with support and confidence.
relation_to_specdx: Mining constraints with support/confidence from many traces is the inverse of SpecDx (which mines where given constraints are violated by many executors); MINERful is also the implementation host of the Di Ciccio et al. inconsistency resolution.

title: Supporting Process Model Validation through Natural Language Generation
authors: Henrik Leopold; Jan Mendling; Artem Polyvyanyy
venue: IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering
subtopics: natural language generation; model validation
summary: Generates natural-language texts from business process models so that domain experts can validate models; generated texts are more complete and structured than manual ones and let readers infer model semantics.
relation_to_specdx: Validation of a formal specification through its NL reading, the reverse direction of SpecDx, which validates T and C by how executors read and act on them.

title: Aligning Event Logs and Process Models for Multi-perspective Conformance Checking: An Approach Based on Integer Linear Programming
authors: Massimiliano de Leoni; Wil M. P. van der Aalst
venue: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
subtopics: multi-perspective conformance; data-aware alignments; ILP
summary: Aligns event logs and process models across control flow, data, resources and time using integer linear programming, so that conformance can be quantified and differences diagnosed beyond control flow.
relation_to_specdx: Data-aware alignment is the BPM counterpart of SpecDx's cells, which are (table,row,column) values read at a scenario step; SpecDx's guardrail clauses over PostgreSQL state are multi-perspective constraints.

title: Conformance Checking Using Cost-Based Fitness Analysis
authors: A. Adriansyah; B.F. van Dongen; W.M.P. van der Aalst
venue: 2011 IEEE 15th International Enterprise Distributed Object Computing Conference
subtopics: alignments; cost-based fitness
summary: Presents a robust replay technique that measures conformance of an event log to a process model with configurable costs for deviations and returns diagnostics about where they occur; the basis of cost-based alignments.
relation_to_specdx: Alignments localise deviations per trace; SpecDx's per-cell deviation counts across a population play the same localising role, with statistical aggregation across executors.

title: Conformance checking of processes based on monitoring real behavior

authors: Timotheus Kampik; Christian Warmuth; Adrian Rebmann; Ron Agam; Lukas N. P. Egger; Andreas Gerber; Johannes Hoffart; Jonas Kolk; Philipp Herzig; Gero Decker; Han van der Aa; Artem Polyvyanyy; Stefanie Rinderle-Ma; Ingo Weber; Matthias Weidlich

authors: Yining Ye; Xin Cong; Shizuo Tian; Jiannan Cao; Hao Wang; Yujia Qin; Yaxi Lu; Heyang Yu; Huadong Wang; Yankai Lin; Zhiyuan Liu; Maosong Sun

title: Conformance checking: a state-of-the-art literature review

title: VERIFAS: a practical verifier for artifact systems

authors: Linh Thao Ly; Fabrizio Maria Maggi; Marco Montali; Stefanie Rinderle-Ma; Wil M.P. van der Aalst

summary: Systematically identifies compliance-monitoring functionalities for business processes (observing violations, fine-grained feedback, prediction) and compares existing approaches and tools against them.

title: Foundations of data-aware process analysis: a database theory perspective
authors: Diego Calvanese; Giuseppe De Giacomo; Marco Montali

summary: Surveys database-theory research on data-aware business processes and argues that this community should provide the formal foundations for analysing processes and data together.

title: Process Model Generation from Natural Language Text
authors: Fabian Friedrich; Jan Mendling; Frank Puhlmann

summary: Generates BPMN process models automatically from natural-language process descriptions (summary from title and venue; the abstract was not accessible).

authors: Maja Pesic; Helen Schonenberg; Wil M.P. van der Aalst
venue: 11th IEEE International Enterprise Distributed Object Computing Conference (EDOC 2007)
subtopics: Declare; declarative process models; LTL
summary: Presents DECLARE, a prototype workflow system for loosely structured processes based on a constraint-based (LTL) declarative modelling language, which keeps features such as model verification and analysis of past executions.
relation_to_specdx: Foundation of Declare clause languages; SpecDx's temporal guardrail clauses can be read as Declare-style constraints.

title: $τ^2$-Bench: Evaluating Conversational Agents in a Dual-Control Environment
authors: Victor Barres; Honghua Dong; Soham Ray; Xujie Si; Karthik R Narasimhan
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306
subtopics: dual-control benchmark; conversational agents; task generator; error separation; agent benchmark; dual control; telecom domain; policy following; policy adherence
summary: Introduces tau2-bench with a dual-control telecom domain (a Dec-POMDP where both user and agent act with tools), a compositional generator of verifiable tasks, a tool-constrained user simulator, and ablations that separate reasoning errors from communication and coordination errors.
relation_to_specdx: Target benchmark family for SpecDx; its later repair (tau2-Bench-Verified, amazon-agi/tau2-bench-verified) supplies real specification defects. tau2-bench attributes failures to agent reasoning versus coordination, never to the task specification. | The specification family on which SpecDx's real defects are defined (τ²-Bench-Verified diff, the Policy Loopholes audit, COBA's findings); SpecDx diagnoses defects in its T (policies) and C (goal states and evaluation criteria). | Its airline and retail policies and task checks are SpecDx's second subject. The compositional task generator is a form of scenario synthesis, but it assumes the policy and checks are correct; SpecDx diagnoses defects in them (cf. the later τ²-Bench-Verified repairs).

title: AgenTracer: Who Is Inducing Failure in the LLM Agentic Systems?
authors: Guibin Zhang; Junhao Wang; Junjie Chen; Wangchunshu Zhou; Kun Wang; Shuicheng YAN
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2026)
subtopics: failure attribution; counterfactual replay; fault injection; trained tracer
summary: AgenTracer annotates failed multi-agent trajectories automatically by counterfactual replay (replace an agent action with a corrected one and re-simulate) and programmed fault injection, producing TracerTraj, and trains AgenTracer-8B with multi-granular RL. It beats large proprietary LLMs on Who&When by up to 18.18% and its feedback improves MetaGPT and MaAS by 4.8-14.2%.
relation_to_specdx: Counterfactual replay is an intervention-based test of a blame hypothesis, close in spirit to SpecDx's refutation by witness; but it presumes the task is solvable and the checker correct, so the earliest flipping correction is always an agent step. SpecDx asks whether any behaviour can satisfy C at all.
baseline_notes: No released code found in the paper's HTML; the replay idea could be re-implemented on SpecDx's executor but it would only ever label agent steps.

title: AgentRx: Diagnosing AI Agent Failures from Execution Trajectories
authors: Shraddha Barke; Arnav Goyal; Alind Khare; Avaljot Singh; Suman Nath; Chetan Bansal
venue: arXiv (accepted to EMNLP Findings 2026 per arXiv comment)
subtopics: failure diagnosis; constraint synthesis; structured API workflows; failure taxonomy
specdx_components: defect taxonomy; baseline B1; baseline B2
summary: Releases 170 manually annotated failed trajectories over 11 settings (structured API workflows, incident management, web/file tasks) with a critical step and a grounded-theory failure category, and AgentRx, which synthesises constraints, checks them step by step into an auditable log of violations with evidence, and lets an LLM judge localise the critical step; step localisation improves by 75% on average.
relation_to_specdx: Synthesises checkable constraints from the task and policy and records clause violations per step, much like SpecDx's per-run violated-clause sets; but it uses one trajectory and assumes the constraints are right, whereas SpecDx treats the clause set as fallible and aggregates violations across a population.
baseline_notes: Released by Microsoft. Run AgentRx on failing SpecDx runs to get the critical step and failure category; cells where AgentRx's critical step coincides across most runs and families are spec-defect candidates. Needs an LLM backend; constraint synthesis could be replaced by SpecDx's own clauses.

title: AgentSuite: Toward More Reliable Agent Evaluation with a Component-Based Benchmark Auditing Pipeline
authors: Hyewon Suh; Binfei Ji; Seojune Lee; Rishi Khare; Basit Khan; Hyunjun Kim; Tianyi Zhang; Venkat Krishna Srinivasan; Peter Belcak; Shizhe Diao; Pavlo Molchanov; Yingyan Celine Lin; Zhen Dong
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306
subtopics: automated benchmark auditing; component taxonomy; tau2-bench audit; validity issues; agent benchmarks; τ²-bench; component-level issue taxonomy
specdx_components: defect taxonomy; baseline B1; real-defect benchmark; baseline B5
summary: COBA decomposes each agent task into User, Environment, Ground Truth and Evaluation components and detects validity issues with hybrid rule-based detectors plus taxonomy-guided LLM evaluation. On six agent benchmarks it reaches F1 0.791-0.874 against experts, finds tau2-bench issues missed by manual verification, and ships in the AgentSuite platform with audited benchmark variants.
relation_to_specdx: The closest published competitor on SpecDx's own target (tau2-bench-style task specifications): automatic, component-localised flaw detection. It reads the artifacts with rules and an LLM rather than executing a population of interpreters, so it gives no satisfaction-based typing, no statistical separation from agent error, and no executed witnesses. | Peer-reviewed (ICML 2026) automatic auditing of the same τ²-bench defects SpecDx targets, so it is the strongest threat to the 'automatic' part of the novelty claim. It combines rules and LLM judgement over task artefacts; it does not execute the specification with a population of interpreters, does not separate defect from agent error statistically, and gives no MUS-based contradiction certificates or refutation witnesses.
baseline_notes: Run COBA (released in AgentSuite) on SpecDx's tau2-style tasks and on seeded mutants; map its component-level issues (Ground Truth, Evaluation, User instruction) to SpecDx's cell/clause locations and defect types to compare recall and localisation. It needs an LLM for the taxonomy-guided step; rule detectors run offline. | Closest published counterpart to B1+B5 combined (static LLM review plus rule-based checks). Inputs per task: user instruction, environment/DB, ground-truth trajectory and evaluation config, which SpecDx's τ²-bench tasks already provide; outputs component-level issue labels mappable to SpecDx's types. Code release not verified; would need porting to local models for an offline run.

title: Automated Transcript Analysis for Detecting Flaws in Agentic Benchmarks
authors: Jeff Mohl; Nelson Gardner-Challis; Magda Dubois; Harry Coppock; Benjamin Allan-Rahill; Kaelan Yim; Damian Sójka; James Mann; Justin Olive
venue: arXiv
subtopics: transcript analysis; benchmark validity; automated scanners; tool failure
summary: Builds LLM scanners over agent transcripts to detect four validity issues (ground-truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, answer-format ambiguity), with human labelling rubrics, and evaluates them on held-out Inspect Evals benchmarks; the scanners found verified issues in five widely used benchmarks, though performance varied by benchmark, criterion and model.
relation_to_specdx: Uses agent transcripts, as SpecDx does, to surface benchmark-side problems, but scans transcripts one at a time with an LLM for predefined issue types; SpecDx aggregates across a population and localises to specification cells and clauses.
baseline_notes: Scanner prompts and evaluation code are released ('ABC inspired Scout scanners'). Adaptation: run the 'answer-format ambiguity' and 'tool failure' scanners over SpecDx run transcripts and aggregate per cell; serves as a transcript-level LLM baseline. LLM backend required.

title: Benchmarking the Benchmarks: A Validity Audit of Tool-Calling Evaluation
authors: Vishvesh Bhat; Jay Vaghasiya; Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin; Asad Aali
venue: arXiv
subtopics: evaluator validity; tool-calling benchmarks; tau2-bench; brittle state matching; run-to-run variance; benchmark validity; tau2-bench defects; evaluator audit
summary: Audits four tool-calling benchmark families (BFCL v4, tau2-Bench, LiveMCPBench, MCP-Atlas) on 496 expert-reviewed tasks and finds 18.5% evaluator-human misalignment: deterministic checkers show brittle state matching, trajectory lock-in, incorrect ground truths and reward-basis misalignment, while LLM-judge benchmarks show rubric drift and large run-to-run variance (scores from 57.9% to 76.8% across 23 repeats). Releases a taxonomy, corrected evaluation components and the Tool-Veritas benchmark.
relation_to_specdx: Documents real hidden-requirement and weak-check defects in tau2-bench's golden-state checks, the class SpecDx targets, via expert review; SpecDx aims to find the same issues automatically from executor populations. | Provides human-audited real defects in τ²-Bench that can serve as SpecDx ground truth and a taxonomy to map onto contradiction/hidden requirement/ambiguity/weak check; its audit is manual, SpecDx's is automatic.
baseline_notes: Its released trace-level audit artifacts on tau2-Bench could serve as an external real-defect test set for SpecDx.
verified_by: arxiv (arxiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02577 (export.arxiv.org API returned HTTP 429))

title: Causal Agent Replay: Counterfactual Attribution for LLM-Agent Failures
authors: Jaineet Shah
venue: arXiv
subtopics: counterfactual replay; structural causal model; Shapley attribution; confidence intervals
summary: Causal Agent Replay models an agent run as a structural causal model, applies do-interventions to steps and re-executes forward under the same stochastic policy to measure shifts in the outcome distribution; it provides a contrastive single-step estimator and a budgeted Monte-Carlo Shapley estimator with confidence intervals, validated on synthetic SCMs, and runs on hosted or local models.
relation_to_specdx: Distributional, executed counterfactuals with confidence intervals are close to SpecDx's sampling-based reasoning; but interventions target agent steps, not specification clauses, so a defective check would be misread as a pivotal agent step.
baseline_notes: Open source and supports free local models. Adaptation: on a SpecDx scenario, intervene on (a) the agent step that wrote a violating cell and (b) the clause in C (drop or relax it) and compare outcome shifts; a large effect only under clause intervention indicates a spec defect. Needs a re-executable environment, which SpecDx's PostgreSQL harness provides.

title: DoVer: Intervention-Driven Auto Debugging for LLM Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Ming Ma; Jue Zhang; Fangkai Yang; Yu Kang; Qingwei Lin; Saravan Rajmohan; Dongmei Zhang
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2026)
subtopics: intervention-based debugging; hypothesis validation; multiple root causes
summary: DoVer argues that log-only failure attribution yields untested hypotheses and that single-step attribution is often ill-posed because several distinct interventions can each repair a failure. It validates attribution hypotheses by targeted interventions (editing messages, altering plans) and re-execution, flipping 18-28% of failed GAIA/AssistantBench trials and validating or refuting 30-60% of hypotheses.
relation_to_specdx: Shares SpecDx's stance that a diagnosis must be tested by execution (validate or refute), but intervenes on agent messages, not on the specification; its finding that blame is not unique echoes SpecDx's set-valued truth.

title: ELT-Bench-Verified: Benchmark Quality Issues Underestimate AI Agent Capabilities
authors: Christopher Zanoli; Andrea Giovannini; Tengjun Jin; Ana Klimovic; Yotam Perlitz
venue: arXiv
subtopics: benchmark repair; LLM root-cause analysis; rigid evaluation scripts; incorrect ground truth; Verified release; agent benchmarks; LLM-driven root-cause audit; data engineering
specdx_components: real-defect benchmark; defect taxonomy; baseline B1
summary: Revisits ELT-Bench (data-pipeline construction agents) and shows capabilities were underestimated: an Auditor-Corrector method combining LLM-driven root-cause analysis of failures with human validation (Fleiss' kappa 0.85) finds that most failed transformation tasks contain benchmark-attributable errors (rigid evaluation scripts, ambiguous specifications, incorrect ground truth); ELT-Bench-Verified fixes them.
relation_to_specdx: A data-engineering, SQL-flavoured benchmark where failures are attributed to the benchmark rather than the agent, exactly SpecDx's dichotomy, with defect classes resembling SpecDx's (ambiguity, mis-keyed ground truth, over-strict checks). Its attribution is per-failure LLM RCA plus humans, not population statistics with logical witnesses. | Shows the three defect families SpecDx types (hidden requirement/incorrect ground truth, ambiguity, over-strict checks) on a SQL/data benchmark close to SpecDx's PostgreSQL setting, and attributes failures to the specification rather than the agent. Its audit is an LLM auditor plus human validation per failed task; SpecDx's diagnosis is statistical over an executor population with logic-based refutation and needs no human validation step.
baseline_notes: The Auditor step (LLM root-cause analysis of each failed run: agent error vs benchmark error) can be re-run on SpecDx's failing runs with T, C and the final DB diff as context; its per-run verdicts aggregated per cell give an RCA baseline. Benchmark code is public; check whether the auditor prompts are released.

title: ImpossibleBench: Measuring LLMs' Propensity of Exploiting Test Cases
authors: Ziqian Zhong; Aditi Raghunathan; Nicholas Carlini
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2026)
subtopics: specification gaming; test exploitation; spec-test conflict; coding agents; specification-test conflict; reward hacking; benchmark
summary: ImpossibleBench creates impossible variants of LiveCodeBench and SWE-bench tasks by introducing direct conflicts between the natural-language specification and the unit tests; any pass implies a specification-violating shortcut, so the pass rate is a cheating rate. Used to study cheating behaviours, context engineering, and monitors.
relation_to_specdx: Its 'impossible' variants are seeded contradictions between T and C, the same construction as a SpecDx mutation operator for the contradiction type. ImpossibleBench measures agent propensity to exploit a known conflict; SpecDx must discover the conflict without knowing it is there, and agents that game the check are a threat to its signal. | Its impossible variants are seeded Tell-vs-Check contradictions, i.e. exactly SpecDx's hidden-requirement/contradiction mutation class; ImpossibleBench uses them to measure agent misbehaviour, whereas SpecDx uses agent behaviour to detect such conflicts, so ImpossibleBench tasks are a ready external evaluation set (each task carries a known seeded conflict).
baseline_notes: Not a detector; its spec-test conflict construction is a template for SpecDx contradiction mutants and its cheating transcripts a stress test.

title: Scalable Weak-to-Strong Verifier Hardening for Agent Environments
authors: Chong Zeng; Ziqian Zhong; Kexun Zhang; Ivan Bercovich; Ivgeni Segal; Yuzhen Mao; Shashwat Saxena; Aditi Raghunathan
venue: arXiv
subtopics: verifier hardening; hacker-fixer loop; weak checks; agent environments
summary: Proposes fully automatic weak-to-strong hardening of programmatic verifiers in agent environments: an isolated verifier sandbox plus a hacker-fixer loop in which agents search for exploits that earn full credit without doing the task and fixers patch the verifier.
relation_to_specdx: Automates the discovery and repair of weak checks via exploit witnesses, overlapping SpecDx's weak-check refutation; it does not address contradictions, hidden requirements or ambiguity and has no population statistics.

title: SpecBench: Measuring Reward Hacking in Long-Horizon Coding Agents
authors: Bingchen Zhao; Dhruv Srikanth; Yuxiang Wu; Zhengyao Jiang
venue: arXiv
subtopics: reward hacking; specification vs visible tests; held-out tests; long-horizon coding
summary: SpecBench decomposes software tasks into a natural-language specification, visible validation tests that exercise features in isolation, and held-out tests that compose those features; the pass-rate gap between visible and held-out tests measures how far long-horizon coding agents optimise the tests instead of the specification.
relation_to_specdx: Makes the T-versus-C gap explicit: visible tests under-constrain the specification (a weak check by construction) and the held-out tests reveal it. SpecDx detects such under-constraining checks without held-out tests, from interpreter disagreement and witness search.

title: Spectrum-Based Failure Attribution for Multi-agent Systems
authors: Yu Ge; Linna Xie; Zhong Li; Yu Pei; Tian Zhang
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (FSE 2026)
subtopics: spectrum-based fault localisation; failure attribution; repeated executions; LLM multi-agent systems
specdx_components: baseline B4; family effects/correlated errors; baseline B3
summary: FAMAS is a spectrum-based failure attribution method for multi-agent systems: it replays a task many times, abstracts the trajectories, and scores each agent action's suspiciousness from how its activation co-varies with failure across the repeated executions, using a formula combining agent and action activation patterns. It beats 12 baselines on Who&When.
relation_to_specdx: Closest methodological neighbour in this theme: it localises blame from statistics over many stochastic executions rather than one trace, as SpecDx does. FAMAS still assumes the task and its oracle are correct and localises to agent actions, whereas SpecDx localises to specification cells and clauses, uses a latent-truth model with anchors rather than SBFL suspiciousness, and adds logical refutation. | Closest SFL work on LLM agents: it also uses repeated stochastic LLM executions as spectra. It attributes failures to agent actions, assumes the task specification is correct, and has no logical (MUS/refutation) component, whereas SpecDx localises defects in the specification itself.
baseline_notes: Can be re-implemented on SpecDx's run matrix: treat each (cell, observed value) or clause-violation event as a 'program element', each run as a test with pass/fail from C, and compute FAMAS/Ochiai-style suspiciousness. Cells with high suspiciousness and failure in nearly all runs across families would be flagged as spec defects. Needs: repeated runs with pass/fail and per-run event spectra (SpecDx already has these). No code repository located; formula is in the paper.

title: Verifying the Verifiers: Failure Attribution for Agentic Benchmark Diagnostics and Training Data Curation
authors: Jesse Hu; Pratyush Shukla; Ke Huang
venue: ICLR 2026 Workshop on AI with Recursive Self-Improvement
subtopics: agent error vs task defect; failure attribution taxonomy; agentic judge with sandbox; RL data curation
summary: Formalises failure attribution for coding-agent benchmarks as deciding whether a failure reflects an agent limitation or a task defect (ambiguous specification, flaky tests, broken environment), validates the taxonomy with human annotation (kappa 0.929), and presents AutoTriage, an agentic judge with sandbox access that executes code and tests; the best configuration reaches kappa 0.833 with humans, while weaker judges over-attribute agent failures to task defects.
relation_to_specdx: States SpecDx's exact dichotomy (agent error vs task defect) and automates it, threatening the novelty of the problem framing. It decides per failed trajectory with one strong judge and sandbox probes; SpecDx decides per specification cell from a population of executors, types the defect, and localises it to a clause or sentence of T. The reported pro-agent bias of weak judges is a useful warning for SpecDx's B1.
baseline_notes: Re-implementable: give an LLM agent sandbox access to the SpecDx PostgreSQL state and tools plus one failing run, ask 'agent error or task defect', aggregate verdicts per cell. No code release was found (workshop paper); the protocol is simple enough to re-create with a local model.

title: What Makes a Terminal-Bench Task Hard? Separating Genuine Hardness from Fake-Hardness on an Adjudicated Agentic Corpus
authors: Edward Lue Chee Lip; Boden Moraski; Tim Knappe; Lang Xiong; Sarvesh Gharat; Antonio Mari; Ivan Bercovich
venue: arXiv
subtopics: all-fail tasks; fake hardness; broken oracles; infrastructure failures; verifier bypass
summary: Studies a frozen Terminal-Bench 3 production record (639 scored tasks, 28,801 trials) and asks what an all-fail task certifies. For 125 tasks with no honest pass, an ordered validity screen over reference-solution runs, empty-solution controls, adversarial trials, trajectories and telemetry keeps only 78 as certified-unsolved; the rest include broken oracles, infrastructure-dominated tasks, verifier bypasses and uncertified solvability.
relation_to_specdx: Squarely on SpecDx's question (a zero pass rate across many agents may be a task defect), using controls such as empty and reference solutions as witnesses. It is a task-level, partly manual screen; SpecDx is cell- and clause-level, statistical over the interpreter population, and types defects.
baseline_notes: The ordered validity screen (reference-solution run, empty-solution control, adversarial trial) is a useful procedural baseline: SpecDx's empty-behaviour and golden-state checks can replicate it, but no code is released.
verified_by: arxiv (arxiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26826 (export.arxiv.org API returned HTTP 429))

title: Who Guards the Benchmarks? Automated Auditing of LLM Agent Benchmarks
authors: Xinming Tu; Tianze Wang; Yingzhou (Minta) Lu; Kexin Huang; Yuanhao Qu; Sara Mostafavi
venue: arXiv (camera-ready for COLM 2026 per arXiv comment; proceedings not yet confirmed)
subtopics: automated benchmark auditing; broken specifications; LLM auditor; execution traces as evidence; cross-artifact verification; agent benchmarks; execution traces
specdx_components: baseline B1; defect taxonomy; real-defect benchmark
summary: BenchGuard uses frontier LLMs to cross-verify all artifacts of execution-based agent benchmarks (instructions, environment, evaluation scripts, reference solutions) through structured protocols, optionally adding agent solutions or traces as evidence. It found 12 author-confirmed issues in ScienceAgentBench, including tasks made unsolvable by fatal errors, and matched 83.3% of expert-found issues on BIXBench Verified-50, at under USD 15 per 50 tasks.
relation_to_specdx: Same goal as SpecDx (find defects in the task specification and its checks, not agent errors) and also uses agent traces as evidence. It differs in method: a single strong LLM auditor reading artifacts, without a population model, typed satisfaction-based defect classes, clause-level localisation via MUS/MCS, or execution-backed witnesses. | Automatic cross-artifact auditing of 'broken specifications, implicit assumptions and rigid evaluation scripts', i.e. contradiction, hidden-requirement and over-strict-check defects, optionally informed by agent traces; it is LLM reasoning over artefacts, not a statistical model over a population of executors, and gives no identifiability guarantees or sound refutation.
baseline_notes: Strongest published counterpart to B1. Run BenchGuard's protocols on SpecDx specifications (T documents, tool descriptions, SQL checks, golden states), with and without SpecDx run traces attached, and score its findings against seeded mutants and real tau2-Bench-Verified defects. Code public (GitHub, licence NOASSERTION); needs a frontier LLM by default, a local model can be swapped in at lower quality. | A stronger B1: feed each task's T and C (and optionally SpecDx's interpreter traces) to its auditing protocol and map its issue reports to SpecDx's types. Code release not yet confirmed; would require frontier-model API access unless the prompts are ported to local models.

title: Agent-as-a-Judge: Evaluate Agents with Agents
authors: Mingchen Zhuge; Changsheng Zhao; Dylan Ashley; Wenyi Wang; Dmitrii Khizbullin; Yunyang Xiong; Zechun Liu; Ernie Chang; Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi; Yuandong Tian; Yangyang Shi; Vikas Chandra; Jürgen Schmidhuber
venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), PMLR 267
subtopics: agent-as-a-judge; trajectory evaluation; requirement satisfaction
summary: Introduces Agent-as-a-Judge, where an agentic system with tools inspects another agent's workspace and trajectory and gives requirement-level feedback, and DevAI, 55 AI-development tasks with 365 hierarchical user requirements. The agent judge outperforms LLM-as-a-judge and approaches human reliability.
relation_to_specdx: Judges whether an agent satisfied each stated requirement, assuming the requirements are right; SpecDx inverts the question and asks which requirement or check is defective given many agents' behaviour.
baseline_notes: Point the released judge (MIT) at each SpecDx run's final DB state and trajectory with T split into requirements, and ask per requirement: satisfied / violated / requirement is unsatisfiable or ambiguous. Disagreement between the judge's verdict and the executable clause C on the same cell, across many runs, flags hidden-requirement or weak-check cells. Needs a tool-using LLM; can run offline on a local model with lower quality.

title: Establishing Best Practices in Building Rigorous Agentic Benchmarks
authors: Yuxuan Zhu; Tengjun Jin; Yada Pruksachatkun; Andy Zhang; Shu Liu; Sasha Cui; Sayash Kapoor; Shayne Longpre; Kevin Meng; Rebecca Weiss; Fazl Barez; Rahul Gupta; Jwala Dhamala; Jacob Merizian; Mario Giulianelli; Harry Coppock; Cozmin Ududec; Antony Kellermann; Jasjeet Sekhon; Jacob Steinhardt; Sarah Schwettmann; Arvind Narayanan; Matei A Zaharia; Ion Stoica; Percy Liang; Daniel Kang
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025)
subtopics: agentic benchmark rigor; benchmark bugs; reward design; checklist; agentic benchmark checklist; task validity; outcome validity; benchmark repair; agentic benchmarks; weak checks; tau-bench; benchmark validity; tau-bench defects
specdx_components: defect taxonomy; real-defect benchmark; baseline B1
summary: Shows that many agentic benchmarks have task-setup or reward-design flaws (e.g. SWE-bench Verified has insufficient tests; tau-bench counts empty responses as successes), which can mis-estimate performance by up to 100% relative, and proposes the Agentic Benchmark Checklist (ABC); applying ABC to CVE-Bench cuts overestimation by 33%.
relation_to_specdx: Documents real weak-check and task-validity defects in tau-bench and SWE-bench and offers a manual checklist; SpecDx aims to find such defects automatically and per clause, with witnesses. | A manual checklist that names the same defect families SpecDx types (weak checks, invalid tasks, wrong outcomes) for agent benchmarks; it relies on expert review, while SpecDx detects and localises such defects automatically from executor behaviour with witnesses. ABC's reported τ-bench and SWE-bench issues are candidate real defects for SpecDx's evaluation. | Documents weak-check defects in tau-bench itself, SpecDx's target setting; ABC is a manual checklist (a B1-like human/LLM review), while SpecDx diagnoses such defects automatically from agent behaviour with witnesses. | Documents weak checks and task defects in τ-bench, supporting SpecDx's motivation; the diagnosis is manual (expert checklist), whereas SpecDx is automatic and typed.
baseline_notes: A manual checklist; its items could be turned into an LLM static-review prompt for B1.

title: TRAIL: Trace Reasoning and Agentic Issue Localization
authors: Darshan Deshpande; Varun Gangal; Hersh Mehta; Jitin Krishnan; Anand Kannappan; Rebecca Qian
venue: arXiv
subtopics: trace debugging; error taxonomy; agentic issue localisation
summary: Proposes a taxonomy of error types in agentic workflow traces (reasoning, system-execution and planning errors) and TRAIL, 148 human-annotated traces from single- and multi-agent systems on software engineering and information retrieval tasks. Long-context LLMs perform poorly at locating errors (best model about 11%).
relation_to_specdx: Localises errors inside one trace, including tool and environment errors, but treats the task as correct. SpecDx localises defects in the specification by contrasting many interpreters on the same cell.

title: Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Shaokun Zhang; Ming Yin; Jieyu Zhang; Jiale Liu; Zhiguang Han; Jingyang Zhang; Beibin Li; Chi Wang; Huazheng Wang; Yiran Chen; Qingyun Wu
venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025), PMLR 267
subtopics: automated failure attribution; multi-agent systems; LLM judge; benchmark; failure attribution; LLM multi-agent systems
specdx_components: baseline B1; defect taxonomy; real-defect benchmark
summary: Formulates automated failure attribution for LLM multi-agent systems (which agent, which decisive step caused the failure) and releases Who&When, failure logs from 127 systems with agent/step annotations. Three LLM-judge attribution methods (all-at-once, step-by-step, binary search) reach at most 53.5% agent accuracy and 14.2% step accuracy.
relation_to_specdx: Shares the goal of localising where a run went wrong, but assumes the task and its checker are correct and always blames an agent step; SpecDx instead asks whether the failure belongs to the specification, using agreement across a population of interpreters rather than one trace. | Diagnoses failures of agents, assuming the task is well specified; SpecDx asks the complementary question of whether the task specification itself is at fault. FAMAS (SFL) is the spectrum-based answer to this benchmark.
baseline_notes: Run the three released Who&When methods (all-at-once, step-by-step, binary search; MIT code, OpenAI-style prompts that can be pointed at a local Ollama model) on each failing SpecDx run trajectory, with the task text T and the violated clause as context. Adaptation: add a third label so the judge can answer 'specification defect' besides naming an agent step, then aggregate per cell (a cell is flagged when most runs' decisive step lands on the same clause and the judge blames the spec). Gives a single-trace LLM-judge counterpart to SpecDx's population statistics; offline-capable with a local model.

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
authors: Mert Cemri; Melissa Z Pan; Shuyi Yang; Lakshya A Agrawal; Bhavya Chopra; Rishabh Tiwari; Kurt Keutzer; Aditya Parameswaran; Dan Klein; Kannan Ramchandran; Matei A Zaharia; Joseph Gonzalez; Ion Stoica
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025), Datasets and Benchmarks Track
subtopics: failure taxonomy; multi-agent systems; LLM-as-a-judge annotation
summary: Builds MAST, a 14-mode failure taxonomy for multi-agent LLM systems in three categories (system design, inter-agent misalignment, task verification), from expert analysis of 150 traces (kappa 0.88), and MAST-Data with 1600+ annotated traces over 7 frameworks. An LLM-as-a-judge annotator scales the labelling.
relation_to_specdx: MAST's 'system design / specification' failure modes (e.g. disobeying task or role specification) are agent-side labels; it does not ask whether the task specification or its checker is itself defective. SpecDx's defect taxonomy (contradiction, hidden requirement, ambiguity, weak check) is defined by satisfaction of the spec, not by agent behaviour.
baseline_notes: The released LLM annotator labels a trace with MAST modes. On SpecDx runs it would output agent-side modes; a run labelled with 'fail to ask for clarification' or 'task verification' failures concentrated on one cell could be read as an ambiguity or weak-check signal. Inputs: a full trace per run. Code is public (no licence file); needs an LLM endpoint, which can be local.

title: A Survey on Evaluation of LLM-based Agents
authors: Asaf Yehudai; Lilach Eden; Alan Li; Guy Uziel; Yilun Zhao; Roy Bar-Haim; Arman Cohan; Michal Shmueli-Scheuer
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026
subtopics: survey; agent evaluation
summary: Surveys evaluation of LLM-based agents across core capabilities (planning, tool use), application benchmarks (web, SWE, conversational), generalist agents, benchmark dimensions, and developer frameworks, identifying gaps in cost-efficiency, safety, robustness and fine-grained, scalable evaluation.
relation_to_specdx: Background survey; benchmark validity and specification defects are not a focus, which supports SpecDx's gap claim.

title: Aegis: Automated Error Generation and Attribution for Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Fanqi Kong; Ruijie Zhang; Huaxiao Yin; Guibin Zhang; Xiaofei Zhang; Ziang Chen; Zhaowei Zhang; Xiaoyuan Zhang; Song-Chun Zhu; Xue Feng
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2026)
subtopics: failure attribution; error injection; synthetic training data
summary: Aegis builds 9,533 multi-agent trajectories with labelled faulty agents and error modes by having an LLM manipulator inject context-aware errors into successful runs, and trains attribution models with SFT, RL and contrastive learning; fine-tuned small models rival much larger proprietary ones.
relation_to_specdx: Seeds errors into agent behaviour to obtain ground truth, analogous to SpecDx seeding defects into the specification with mutation operators; Aegis's seeded faults are agent errors only.

title: Beyond Resolution Rates: Behavioral Drivers of Coding Agent Success and Failure
authors: Tural Mehtiyev; Wesley Assunção
venue: arXiv
subtopics: cross-agent study; never-solved tasks; SWE-bench Verified; behavioural drivers
summary: Analyses 9,374 trajectories from 19 agents (8 frameworks, 14 LLMs) on the same 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks; finds that patch complexity does not explain difficulty (12 never-solved tasks need only simple patches) and that the trajectory-length/failure correlation reverses once task difficulty is controlled.
relation_to_specdx: Provides exactly the population-over-tasks matrix SpecDx exploits, and attributes all-agent failures on simple tasks to agent reasoning gaps; SpecDx would treat such consistent, cross-family failure as a candidate specification defect and test it.
baseline_notes: Its multi-agent trajectory corpus could be re-analysed with SpecDx's consensus signature.

title: Conformal Agent Error Attribution
authors: Naihe Feng; Yi Sui; Shiyi Hou; Ga Wu; Jesse C. Cresswell
venue: arXiv
subtopics: conformal prediction; error attribution; finite-sample guarantees; rollback
summary: Frames multi-agent error attribution with conformal prediction, giving finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees, with new filtration-based CP algorithms that predict contiguous step intervals in a trajectory; prediction sets are used to roll the system back and let it correct its own errors.
relation_to_specdx: One of few attribution works with finite-sample statistical guarantees, comparable in spirit to SpecDx's Hoeffding bounds; the guarantee is about locating an agent error step, not about separating spec defects from agent errors.

title: Faults in Our Formal Benchmarking: Dataset Defects and Evaluation Failures in Lean Theorem Proving
authors: Pawan Sasanka Ammanamanchi; Siddharth Bhat; Stella Biderman
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306
subtopics: specification defects; formal benchmarks; certified counterexamples; static checkers
summary: Audits five Lean theorem-proving benchmarks with corpus-scale static checkers, surfacing 4,833 findings including 398 mechanically certified issues (counterexamples, vacuous theorems, unsound axioms), plus semantic defects where the formal statement does not faithfully encode the informal problem; shows defects both inflate and deflate prover scores and releases checkers and audit prompts.
relation_to_specdx: A formal-methods analogue of SpecDx: the checked statement (C) may not match the informal problem (T), and defects are certified by machine-checked witnesses. It relies on static checkers and prompts rather than a population of executors.

title: Finding Blind Spots in AppWorld and WorkArena Task Verifiers
authors: Richard Abrich
venue: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Who Verifies the Agents? Toward Reliable Agent Development
subtopics: weak checks; verifier mutation testing; stateful API benchmarks
summary: Audits execution-based task verifiers in AppWorld and WorkArena with source-informed mutation testing, finding blind spots such as duplicated non-idempotent writes that still pass AppWorld checks and incorrect persisted values that WorkArena checkers miss.
relation_to_specdx: Finds weak checks in database-state verifiers by mutating behaviours, the same 'wrong behaviour passes every clause' witness SpecDx's weak-check refutation produces; here the mutations are hand-designed from verifier source, not driven by an interpreter population.

title: Holistic Agent Leaderboard: The Missing Infrastructure for AI Agent Evaluation
authors: Sayash Kapoor; Benedikt Stroebl; Peter Kirgis; Nitya Nadgir; Zachary Siegel; Boyi Wei; Tianci Xue; Ziru Chen; Felix Chen; Saiteja Utpala; Franck Ndzomga; Dheeraj Oruganty; Sophie Luskin; Kangheng Liu; Botao Yu; Amit Arora; Dongyoon Hahm; Harsh Trivedi; Huan Sun; Juyong Lee; Tengjun Jin; Yifan Mai; Yifei Zhou; Yuxuan Zhu; Rishi Bommasani; Daniel Kang; Dawn Song; Peter Henderson; Yu Su; Percy Liang; Arvind Narayanan
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2026)
subtopics: agent leaderboard; evaluation infrastructure; log inspection; reproducibility
summary: Presents the Holistic Agent Leaderboard: a standardised harness running parallel evaluations across hundreds of VMs, a three-way analysis of 21,730 rollouts over 9 models and 9 benchmarks (including customer service), and LLM-aided log inspection that surfaces unreported behaviours such as searching for the benchmark answers online. All logs are released.
relation_to_specdx: Provides multi-model rollouts on the same tasks, the raw material SpecDx needs, and uses LLM log inspection to find odd behaviour, but does not separate task defects from agent errors statistically. HAL's released logs (including tau-bench) could serve as an external population for SpecDx.
baseline_notes: Not a method; its released multi-model logs are a possible extra data source (repository archived).

title: RAFFLES: Reasoning-based Attribution of Faults for LLM Systems
authors: Chenyang Zhu; Spencer Hong; Jingyu Wu; Kushal Chawla; Yuhui Tang; Youbing Yin; Nathan Wolfe; Erin Babinsky; Daben Liu
venue: Proceedings of the 19th Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
subtopics: failure attribution; iterative judge; evaluator ensemble
summary: RAFFLES is an offline, iterative evaluation architecture in which a central Judge proposes candidate faults and specialised Evaluators critique the faults and the Judge's rationale, applied to step-level fault finding on Who&When and on ReasonEval mathematical reasoning.
relation_to_specdx: Another LLM-judge attribution pipeline that assumes the task is valid; relevant only as an alternative single-trace judge baseline.

title: Rethinking Failure Attribution in Multi-Agent Systems: A Multi-Perspective Benchmark and Evaluation
authors: Yeonjun In; Mehrab Tanjim; Jayakumar Subramanian; Sungchul Kim; Uttaran Bhattacharya; Wonjoong Kim; Sangwu Park; Somdeb Sarkhel; Chanyoung Park
venue: arXiv
subtopics: multi-perspective attribution; attribution ambiguity; benchmark design
summary: Argues that multi-agent failures often admit several plausible attributions and that single-root-cause benchmarks distort conclusions; proposes multi-perspective failure attribution, the MP-Bench benchmark and an evaluation protocol, and finds that earlier claims that LLMs cannot attribute failures stem largely from benchmark design.
relation_to_specdx: Accepts set-valued ground truth for blame, which parallels SpecDx's set-valued entailment sets A_c; still confined to agent-side attribution.

title: Seeing the Whole Elephant: A Benchmark for Failure Attribution in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Mengzhuo Chen; Junjie Wang; Fangwen Mu; Yawen Wang; Zhe Liu; Huanxiang Feng; Qing Wang
venue: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
subtopics: failure attribution benchmark; full observability; reproducible environments
summary: Argues that Who&When-style benchmarks expose only agent outputs, and introduces TraceElephant with full execution traces (inputs and context) and reproducible environments; full traces improve attribution accuracy by up to 76% over partial observation.
relation_to_specdx: Reproducible environments allow re-execution, the precondition for SpecDx-style refutation; the benchmark still labels agent steps only.

title: SWE-Bench Pro Verified: A Reliable Benchmark for Software Engineering Agents
authors: Pujun Zheng; Zixin Shang; Shufan Jiang; Wenhui Tian; Dongsheng Zhu; Zerun Ma; Dingbo Yuan; Qi Zhang
venue: arXiv
subtopics: benchmark repair; misleading problem statements; improperly scoped tests; gold-solution leakage
summary: Shows SWE-Bench Pro is undermined by reward hacking through leaked gold solutions or hidden evaluation information and by task-quality issues (misleading statements, improperly scoped tests), and releases SWE-Bench Pro Verified with anti-hacking safeguards and minimal task corrections; some models score substantially lower.
relation_to_specdx: Another curated set of real ambiguity and over/under-constrained-test defects in an agent benchmark; repairs are curated rather than inferred.
verified_by: arxiv (arxiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08149 (export.arxiv.org API returned HTTP 429))

title: Talk, Evaluate, Diagnose: User-aware Agent Evaluation with Automated Error Analysis
authors: Penny Chong; Harshavardhan Abichandani; Jiyuan SHEN; Atin Ghosh; Min Moe; Yifan Mai; Daniel Dahlmeier
venue: International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2026)
subtopics: conversational agent evaluation; LLM-as-a-judge; automated error analysis; user personas
summary: TED evaluates conversational tool agents with expert and non-expert user personas, rewrites subgoals of existing datasets as natural-language grading notes scored by an LLM judge with new efficiency and progress metrics, and adds an automated error-analysis tool that mines inconsistencies between judge and agents to surface common errors.
relation_to_specdx: Its diagnosis step analyses judge-agent inconsistencies, a weak analogue of SpecDx's spec-as-fallible-rater anchor; but errors are attributed to agents, and grading notes are assumed correct.

title: Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability
authors: Stephan Rabanser; Sayash Kapoor; Peter Kirgis; Kangheng Liu; Saiteja Utpala; Arvind Narayanan
venue: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306
subtopics: agent reliability metrics; consistency across runs; robustness; calibration
summary: Proposes a reliability profile of twelve metrics along consistency, robustness, predictability and safety, grounded in safety-critical engineering, and evaluates 15 models on two benchmarks: accuracy gains have brought only small reliability gains, and agents remain inconsistent across runs and poorly calibrated.
relation_to_specdx: Treats run-to-run inconsistency as an agent property; SpecDx uses the same repeated-run variation, but decomposes it into agent error and specification-induced deviation.

title: TrajAudit: Automated Failure Diagnosis for Agentic Coding Systems
authors: Minxing Wang; Xiaofei Xie; Yintong Huo
venue: arXiv
subtopics: automated failure diagnosis; coding agents; investigator agent; trajectory reduction
summary: TrajAudit diagnoses failures in long, noisy trajectories of repository-level coding agents with an investigator agent supported by modules that reduce low-signal observations and track the causal chain of failure.
relation_to_specdx: LLM root-cause diagnosis of single coding-agent trajectories; does not consider the task specification or tests as a possible root cause.

title: Who&When Pro: Can LLMs Really Attribute Failures in AI Agents?
authors: Jiale Liu; Huajun Xi; Shaokun Zhang; Yifan Zeng; Tianwei Yue; Chi Wang; Jian Kang; Qingyun Wu; Huazheng Wang
venue: arXiv
subtopics: failure attribution benchmark; controlled fault injection; cross-modality
summary: Who&When Pro is a large failure-attribution benchmark of 12,326 failed trajectories over 3 modalities and 26 benchmarks, built by exactly replaying a successful prefix and then injecting one failure so the golden label is known; analyses show systematic attribution patterns across modalities, protocols and model families.
relation_to_specdx: Uses controlled injection to obtain ground truth, as SpecDx does with specification mutants; the injected faults are agent errors and the task is assumed correct.

title: Abduct, Act, Predict: Scaffolding Causal Inference for Automated Failure Attribution in Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Alva West; Yixuan Weng; Minjun Zhu; Zhen Lin; Zhiyuan Ning; Yue Zhang
venue: arXiv
subtopics: failure attribution; counterfactual reasoning; causal scaffolding
summary: A2P (Abduct-Act-Predict) scaffolds an LLM to infer a hidden root cause, propose a minimal corrective intervention, and predict whether the corrected trajectory would succeed, all in one pass, more than doubling step-level attribution accuracy on Who&When (47.46% and 29.31% on the two subsets).
relation_to_specdx: Simulated counterfactuals inside the LLM rather than executed ones; still blames agent steps. A useful prompt template if the 'intervention' is allowed to edit the specification instead of the agent's action.
baseline_notes: Released MIT code is a prompting scaffold over Who&When logs. Adaptation: feed a failing SpecDx run plus T and C, and allow the Act step to propose an edit to a clause or to T; if the predicted outcome flips only under a spec edit, label the cell a spec defect. Runs with any LLM endpoint including local Ollama.
verified_by: arxiv (arxiv abs page https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.10401 (export.arxiv.org API returned HTTP 429))

title: AgentRewardBench: Evaluating Automatic Evaluations of Web Agent Trajectories
authors: Xing Han Lù; Amirhossein Kazemnejad; Nicholas Meade; Arkil Patel; Dongchan Shin; Alejandra Zambrano; Karolina Stańczak; Peter Shaw; Christopher J. Pal; Siva Reddy
venue: arXiv
subtopics: LLM judges for trajectories; web agents; rule-based evaluation under-reporting
summary: AgentRewardBench has experts review web-agent trajectories from five benchmarks for success, side effects and repetitiveness, and evaluates 12 LLM judges against them: no judge excels everywhere, and the rule-based checks used by benchmarks tend to under-report success.
relation_to_specdx: Evidence that rule-based checks are often too strict (hidden requirements or mis-keyed checks rejecting valid behaviour), and that LLM judges are unreliable replacements; SpecDx diagnoses the check itself rather than replacing it with a judge.

title: AI Agents That Matter
authors: Sayash Kapoor; Benedikt Stroebl; Zachary S. Siegel; Nitya Nadgir; Arvind Narayanan
venue: Transactions on Machine Learning Research
subtopics: agent evaluation practice; reproducibility; holdout sets
summary: Critiques agent benchmarking: a narrow focus on accuracy without cost, conflation of model-developer and downstream-developer needs, inadequate holdout sets that let agents take shortcuts, and poor standardisation that undermines reproducibility. Proposes cost-accuracy joint optimisation.
relation_to_specdx: Motivates treating agent benchmark results as noisy measurements; it does not diagnose defects inside individual task specifications, which is SpecDx's target.

title: An Empirical Study on Failures in Automated Issue Solving
authors: Simiao Liu; Fang Liu; Liehao Li; Xin Tan; Yinghao Zhu; Xiaoli Lian; Li Zhang
venue: arXiv
subtopics: SWE-bench failure taxonomy; issue solving; manual failure analysis
summary: Compares three state-of-the-art pipeline and agentic issue-solving tools on SWE-bench Verified and manually analyses 150 failed instances, deriving a failure taxonomy with 3 phases, 9 categories and 25 subcategories of failure modes.
relation_to_specdx: An agent-side failure taxonomy for SE agents; failures are attributed to tool behaviour rather than to task or test defects.

title: EvilGenie: A Reward Hacking Benchmark
authors: Jonathan Gabor; Jayson Lynch; Jonathan Rosenfeld
venue: arXiv
subtopics: reward hacking; coding agents; test-file editing; hardcoded tests
summary: EvilGenie is a reward-hacking benchmark built from LiveCodeBench problems in an environment where agents can easily hack (hardcode test cases, edit test files); hacking is measured with held-out tests, LLM judges and test-edit detection, and explicit reward hacking is observed in Codex and Claude Code.
relation_to_specdx: Shows that agents exploit checks when the task is hard; in SpecDx such exploitation would make a weak or contradictory check look satisfied, so gaming behaviour must be separated from faithful readings.

title: Understanding Software Engineering Agents: A Study of Thought-Action-Result Trajectories
authors: Islem Bouzenia; Michael Pradel
venue: 2025 40th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE)
subtopics: SWE agent trajectories; failure modes; empirical study
summary: Large-scale empirical study of thought-action-result trajectories of RepairAgent, AutoCodeRover and OpenHands (120 trajectories, 2,822 LLM interactions) on program repair and issue resolution, combining quantitative analysis of action patterns and token use with qualitative assessment of reasoning coherence and feedback use, to characterise failure behaviour.
relation_to_specdx: Characterises agent-side failure behaviour of SE agents; it does not consider whether the issue or its tests are defective.

title: Where Did It All Go Wrong? A Hierarchical Look into Multi-Agent Error Attribution
authors: Adi Banerjee; Anirudh Nair; Tarik Borogovac
venue: arXiv
subtopics: failure attribution; consensus voting; hierarchical context
summary: ECHO improves agent/step error attribution in multi-agent traces over all-at-once, step-by-step and binary-search baselines by combining a hierarchical, position-based context representation, objective analysis by several specialised judge agents, and confidence-weighted consensus voting.
